library(tidyverse)

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 2.1 summarize(): many rows in, one row out
text:
2.1 summarize(): many rows in, one row out

movies |>
  summarize(avg_score = mean(audience_score))

#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   avg_score
#>       <dbl>
#> 1      62.4


You can compute several summaries at once. Name each one on the left of =.

movies |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    avg_score = mean(audience_score),
    median_score = median(audience_score),
    sd_score = sd(audience_score),
    best_imdb = max(imdb_rating),
    n_studios = n_distinct(studio)
  )

#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>       n avg_score median_score sd_score best_imdb n_studios
#>   <int>     <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <int>
#> 1   651      62.4           65     20.2         9       212


Summary functions you will use constantly:







Function
Returns




n()
number of rows (only inside summarize(), mutate(), filter())


n_distinct(x)
number of different values


mean(x), median(x)
center


sd(x), IQR(x)
spread


min(x), max(x)
extremes


sum(x)
total; on a logical vector, the count of TRUE


mean(x) on a logical vector
the proportion of TRUE


first(x), last(x)
first or last value




# How many films are Best Picture nominees, and what share is that?
movies |>
  summarize(
    n_nominated = sum(best_pic_nom == "yes"),
    share = mean(best_pic_nom == "yes")
  )

#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   n_nominated  share
#>         <int>  <dbl>
#> 1          22 0.0338

section: 2.3 group_by() + summarize(): one row per group
text:
2.3 group_by() + summarize(): one row per group

movies |>
  group_by(genre) |>
  summarize(n = n(), avg_score = mean(audience_score)) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_score))

#> # A tibble: 11 x 3
#>   genre                         n avg_score
#>   <chr>                     <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Documentary                  52      82.8
#> 2 Musical & Performing Arts    12      80.2
#> 3 Other                        16      66.7
#> 4 Drama                       305      65.3
#> 5 Art House & International    14      64  
#> 6 Animation                     9      62.4
#> # i 5 more rows


Read it as: “For each genre, count the films and average the audience score; then sort.”






Key idea



A grouped summary has one row per group and one column per summary. Before you trust any grouped result, ask: what is a row now?








Audit it: an average without its n



In the table above, Documentary has the highest average (82.8) with 52 films, and Musical & Performing Arts is second with only 12. Always print n() next to a mean. An average of a handful of rows is far less stable than an average of hundreds.

movies |> count(genre, sort = TRUE)

section: 2.5 Several grouping columns, and what .groups does
text:
2.5 Several grouping columns, and what .groups does

by_two <- movies |>
  group_by(genre, mpaa_rating) |>
  summarize(n = n(), avg_score = mean(audience_score))
by_two

#> # A tibble: 44 x 4
#> # Groups:   genre [11]
#>   genre              mpaa_rating     n avg_score
#>   <chr>              <chr>       <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Action & Adventure G               5      70.2
#> 2 Action & Adventure PG             21      49.3
#> 3 Action & Adventure PG-13          17      40.6
#> 4 Action & Adventure R              22      64.5
#> 5 Animation          G               6      58.3
#> 6 Animation          PG              3      70.7
#> # i 38 more rows


When you group by two columns, summarize() removes only the last group, which might be inconvenient. The result is still grouped by genre, so later verbs will quietly work per genre. The .groups argument allows controlling the resulting grouping structure:

movies |>
  group_by(genre, mpaa_rating) |>
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop") # plain table, no leftover groups

#> # A tibble: 44 x 3
#>   genre              mpaa_rating     n
#>   <chr>              <chr>       <int>
#> 1 Action & Adventure G               5
#> 2 Action & Adventure PG             21
#> 3 Action & Adventure PG-13          17
#> 4 Action & Adventure R              22
#> 5 Animation          G               6
#> 6 Animation          PG              3
#> # i 38 more rows








Audit it: hidden groups change later steps



Suppose an AI continues the pipeline that generated by_two with mutate(share = n / sum(n)). The denominator is the total within each genre, not across the whole table, because by_two is still grouped by genre.

by_two |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |> # share within genre, because groups remain
  select(genre, mpaa_rating, n, share) |>
  head(4)

#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#> # Groups:   genre [1]
#>   genre              mpaa_rating     n  share
#>   <chr>              <chr>       <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Action & Adventure G               5 0.0769
#> 2 Action & Adventure PG             21 0.323 
#> 3 Action & Adventure PG-13          17 0.262 
#> 4 Action & Adventure R              22 0.338


Whether that is what you wanted depends on the question. The point is to know. Check for Groups: in the printout, and finish with ungroup() or .groups = "drop".

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
2.6 The shortcut: .by
In dplyr 1.1 and later, summarize(), mutate(), filter(), and slice_*() accept .by. It groups for that one verb only, and it never leaves hidden groups behind.

movies |>
  summarize(avg_score = mean(audience_score), .by = genre) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_score)) |>
  head(4)

#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   genre                     avg_score
#>   <chr>                         <dbl>
#> 1 Documentary                    82.8
#> 2 Musical & Performing Arts      80.2
#> 3 Other                          66.7
#> 4 Drama                          65.3


Both styles are correct and you will see both in AI output. .by is shorter and safer. group_by() is more familiar and reads well when several steps share the same grouping.

movies |>
  summarize(

section: 2.10 Top or bottom rows per group with slice_*()
text:
2.10 Top or bottom rows per group with slice_*()

movies |>
  slice_max(imdb_rating, n = 1, by = genre) |>
  select(genre, title, imdb_rating)

#> # A tibble: 12 x 3
#>   genre                     title                   imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                     <chr>                         <dbl>
#> 1 Drama                     The Prestige                    8.5
#> 2 Comedy                    Annie Hall                      8.1
#> 3 Horror                    Phantom of the Paradise         7.4
#> 4 Documentary               Promises                        8.5
#> 5 Action & Adventure        Aliens                          8.4
#> 6 Art House & International The Ritz                        7.8
#> # i 6 more rows








Audit it: ties give you extra rows



There are 11 genres, but the result above has 12 rows, because two Musical & Performing Arts films tie at 7.9. slice_max() keeps ties by default. Add with_ties = FALSE to get exactly one row per genre (it then keeps the first in the data’s order, so decide whether that is fair).

movies |>
  slice_max(imdb_rating, n = 1, by = genre, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  nrow()

#> [1] 11










Audit it: the average of averages



After a grouped summary, an AI is often asked for “the overall average” and averages the group averages. That gives a 9-film genre the same weight as a 305-film genre.

genre_means <- movies |> summarize(avg = mean(audience_score), .by = genre)

mean(genre_means$avg) # mean of the group means

#> [1] 61.85006

mean(movies$audience_score) # the real overall mean

#> [1] 62.36252


If you need an overall figure from group summaries, you need a weighted mean (weighted.mean(avg, n)) or you should go back to the original rows.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
2.11 A full pipeline, read aloud

movies |>
  filter(title_type == "Feature Film") |>
  group_by(genre) |>
  summarize(n = n(), avg_score = mean(audience_score)) |>
  filter(n >= 20) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_score))

#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>   genre                  n avg_score
#>   <chr>              <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Drama                301      65.3
#> 2 Mystery & Suspense    59      55.9
#> 3 Action & Adventure    65      53.8
#> 4 Comedy                85      51.8
#> 5 Horror                23      45.8


“Keep feature films. For each genre, count the films and average the audience score. Keep genres with at least 20 films. Sort from highest to lowest.” If you cannot say a pipeline in one breath like this, break it into steps and run each one.






Checklist for any grouped summary




What is a row in the input, and what is a row in the output?
Grouped by what? The right level? Any hidden groups left?
What happened to NA? Dropped, kept, or ignored? How many?
How big is each group? Is n shown?
Is a mean of means hiding in there?

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 3.1 left_join(): keep every row on the left
text:
3.1 left_join(): keep every row on the left

joined <- movies |>
  left_join(studios, by = "studio")

joined |>
  select(title, studio, studio_group, major)

#> # A tibble: 651 x 4
#>   title                studio                   studio_group major
#>   <chr>                <chr>                    <chr>        <lgl>
#> 1 Filly Brown          Indomina Media Inc.      <NA>         NA   
#> 2 The Dish             Warner Bros. Pictures    Warner Bros. TRUE 
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman  Sony Pictures Classics   Sony         TRUE 
#> 4 The Age of Innocence Columbia Pictures        Sony         TRUE 
#> 5 Malevolence          Anchor Bay Entertainment <NA>         NA   
#> 6 Old Partner          Shcalo Media Group       <NA>         NA   
#> # i 645 more rows


left_join(x, y) keeps all rows of x, and adds the columns of y from the matching row. Where there is no match, the new columns are NA.






The row-count rule



When the key is unique in the right table, a left_join() must return exactly as many rows as the left table. Make this a habit:

nrow(movies)

#> [1] 651

nrow(joined)

#> [1] 651


If the numbers differ, stop and find out why before doing anything else.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
3.2 Unmatched rows and anti_join()

joined |>
  count(is.na(studio_group))

#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   `is.na(studio_group)`     n
#>   <lgl>                 <int>
#> 1 FALSE                   402
#> 2 TRUE                    249


249 films have no studio_group. Either their studio is not in the lookup, or their studio is missing. anti_join() returns the rows of the left table that have no match, which is your to-do list for improving the lookup.

movies |>
  anti_join(studios, by = "studio") |>
  count(studio, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(6)

#> # A tibble: 6 x 2
#>   studio                         n
#>   <chr>                      <int>
#> 1 <NA>                           8
#> 2 First Run Features             6
#> 3 Orion Home Video               5
#> 4 Orion Pictures Corporation     4
#> 5 Fox                            3
#> 6 Fox Searchlight Pictures       3








Audit it: inner_join() silently drops rows



inner_join() keeps only rows that match in both tables.

nrow(movies)

#> [1] 651

movies |> inner_join(studios, by = "studio") |> nrow()

#> [1] 402


651 films became 402. There is no error and no warning. Use inner_join() only when dropping unmatched rows is exactly what you want, and say so in a comment.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
3.3 Joining, then summarizing
Once the key is cleaned, the grouped summary answers a different question than the raw column did.

joined |>
  filter(!is.na(studio_group)) |>
  summarize(n = n(), avg_score = mean(audience_score), .by = studio_group) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_score)) |>
  head(6)

#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   studio_group     n avg_score
#>   <chr>        <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 HBO              8      68.6
#> 2 Magnolia         9      67.6
#> 3 Weinstein        7      65.3
#> 4 Focus            4      65  
#> 5 Lionsgate       11      64.5
#> 6 Universal       36      64.3


Compare with grouping by the raw studio column: Warner Bros. films were split across several spellings, and no single one of them showed the group’s total.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 3.5 Duplicate keys: how a join invents rows
text:
3.5 Duplicate keys: how a join invents rows
Suppose someone “updates” the lookup, and Paramount Pictures ends up listed twice with different group labels.

studios_v2 <- bind_rows(
  studios,
  tibble(
    studio = "Paramount Pictures",
    studio_group = "Paramount Classics",
    major = TRUE
  )
)

nrow(movies)

#> [1] 651

movies |> left_join(studios_v2, by = "studio") |> nrow()

#> [1] 688


651 became 688. Every Paramount Pictures film (there are 37) matched two rows of the lookup, so it appeared twice. Every later count or average now double counts those films.
Find the duplicate key by counting keys in the lookup:

studios_v2 |>
  count(studio) |>
  filter(n > 1)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   studio                 n
#>   <chr>              <int>
#> 1 Paramount Pictures     2








Audit it: an AI that reports ‘joined successfully’



This is the most important join bug, because nothing crashes. In recent dplyr versions you may see a warning about an “unexpected many-to-many relationship”, but in a script, an R Markdown document, or a long log it is easy to miss. Never accept “no issues” without comparing the row counts.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
3.6 Make R refuse bad joins
The relationship argument states what you expect. If the data disagree, R stops with an error.

movies |>
  left_join(studios_v2, by = "studio", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  nrow()

#> Error in `left_join()`:
#> ! Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`.
#> i Row 18 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.









relationship =
Meaning




"one-to-one"
each row on either side matches at most one row on the other


"many-to-one"
each left row matches at most one right row (our lookup case)


"one-to-many"
each right row matches at most one left row


"many-to-many"
duplicates on both sides are expected



A second guard, unmatched, makes an inner_join() stop instead of silently dropping rows:

movies |>
  inner_join(studios, by = "studio", unmatched = "error")

#> Error in `inner_join()`:
#> ! Each row of `x` must have a match in `y`.
#> i Row 1 of `x` does not have a match.


The error is informative: we already know 249 films have no lookup entry. (For left_join(), unmatched = "error" checks the other direction: it stops if some rows of the lookup would be dropped because no left row uses them.)

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
3.7 Join checklist






Before and after every join




Keys unique on the lookup side? count(key) |> filter(n > 1) should return nothing.
Row count as expected? Compare nrow() before and after.
New NAs? anti_join() shows which keys failed to match.
Right join type? left keeps all left rows, inner drops unmatched rows.
Keys really equal? Extra spaces, capital letters, and spelling variants will not match (see the next box).









Audit it: keys that look equal but are not



Joins compare keys exactly. A trailing space or a different case means no match.

messy <- tibble(
  studio = c("Paramount Pictures", "Paramount Pictures ", "paramount pictures")
)

messy |> left_join(studios, by = "studio")

#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>   studio                studio_group major
#>   <chr>                 <chr>        <lgl>
#> 1 "Paramount Pictures"  Paramount    TRUE 
#> 2 "Paramount Pictures " <NA>         NA   
#> 3 "paramount pictures"  <NA>         NA


Only the first row matched. Cleaning keys (trimming, lowercasing, standardizing spellings) is the subject of Sessions 5 and 6. Here is a preview:

studios_clean <- studios |> mutate(key = str_to_lower(str_squish(studio)))

messy |>
  mutate(key = str_to_lower(str_squish(studio))) |>
  left_join(select(studios_clean, key, studio_group), by = "key")

#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>   studio                key                studio_group
#>   <chr>                 <chr>              <chr>       
#> 1 "Paramount Pictures"  paramount pictures Paramount   
#> 2 "Paramount Pictures " paramount pictures Paramount   
#> 3 "paramount pictures"  paramount pictures Paramount

text:
4.1 pivot_longer(): columns into rows

scores_long <- scores |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(critics_score, audience_score), # which columns to stack
    names_to = "source", # new column for the old column names
    values_to = "score" # new column for the values
  )
scores_long

#> # A tibble: 1,302 x 3
#>   title               source         score
#>   <chr>               <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown         critics_score     45
#> 2 Filly Brown         audience_score    73
#> 3 The Dish            critics_score     96
#> 4 The Dish            audience_score    81
#> 5 Waiting for Guffman critics_score     91
#> 6 Waiting for Guffman audience_score    91
#> # i 1,296 more rows


Now one summarize() handles both score types:

movies |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(critics_score, audience_score),
    names_to = "source",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  summarize(avg = mean(score), .by = c(genre, source)) |>
  arrange(genre) |>
  head(6)

#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   genre                     source           avg
#>   <chr>                     <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 Action & Adventure        critics_score   41.4
#> 2 Action & Adventure        audience_score  53.8
#> 3 Animation                 critics_score   50.2
#> 4 Animation                 audience_score  62.4
#> 5 Art House & International critics_score   51.6
#> 6 Art House & International audience_score  64


Long tables are also what ggplot2 expects (next session): one column to map to color, one to map to the y-axis.
To select columns by pattern instead of listing them, use helpers such as starts_with(), ends_with(), and contains():

movies |>
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("actor"),
    names_to = "billing",
    values_to = "actor"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(actor)) |>
  count(actor, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(5)

#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   actor                 n
#>   <chr>             <int>
#> 1 Richard Gere          8
#> 2 Samuel L. Jackson     8
#> 3 Diane Keaton          7
#> 4 Helen Hunt            7
#> 5 Jamie Foxx            7


The billing column holds actor1 to actor5. names_prefix = "actor" would strip the prefix and leave just the numbers.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 5.1 When the data does not fit in memory
text:
5.1 When the data does not fit in memory
R normally loads a whole table into memory. For a log with hundreds of millions of rows, that is impossible. Our simulated viewing log is small enough to practice on:



Format
Rows
Size on disk




CSV
4,000,000
about 239 MB


Parquet (zstd compression)
4,000,000
about 40 MB



Loading the same data with read_csv() takes about 229 MB of R memory. A real log may be 100 times bigger.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
5.2 What is Parquet?
Parquet is a file format built for analytics.

Columnar: values of one column are stored together, so R reads only the columns a query needs.
Typed: dates stay dates, integers stay integers. (A CSV is text, so every read re-guesses the types.)
Compressed: much smaller than CSV, so it is faster to move and store.
Self-describing: the schema is stored inside the file.

Apache Arrow is the in-memory counterpart, and the arrow package lets you work with Parquet files from R using the dplyr verbs you already know.

install.packages("arrow") # once
library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)

The columns of views.parquet are view_id, title (a movie from movies.csv), user_id, country, device, view_date, minutes (minutes watched), and completed (watched at least 90% of the runtime). All values are simulated.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
5.3 open_dataset(): look without loading

views <- open_dataset("data/views.parquet")

open_dataset() reads only the file’s metadata (the schema), not the 4 million rows. You can check the shape without loading anything:

nrow(views) # 4000000
ncol(views) # 8
names(views)

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 5.4 Lazy evaluation: a query is a recipe
text:
5.4 Lazy evaluation: a query is a recipe
With a Dataset, dplyr verbs do not run. They record what you asked for. Nothing is computed until you call collect().

q <- views |>
  filter(country == "US") |>
  count(device)
# q is a query (a recipe), not a table of results

collect() runs the recipe inside arrow and brings only the result into R.

q |>
  collect() |>
  arrange(desc(n))

#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   device      n
#>   <chr>   <int>
#> 1 TV     684180
#> 2 Phone  380514
#> 3 Laptop 334049
#> 4 Tablet 121455
Arrow scanned 4 million rows. Only 4 rows came into R. Sorting the small result with arrange() after collect() is a good habit, because the row order that arrow returns is not guaranteed.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 5.5 The same verbs from Section 2 and 3 work here

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 5.6 collect() last: the most important rule
text:
5.6 collect() last: the most important rule
Compare these two pipelines. They give the same answer.

# Pipeline A: collect first
views |> collect() |> filter(country == "US") |> count(device)

# Pipeline B: collect last
views |> filter(country == "US") |> count(device) |> collect()

Pipeline A pulls every row into R (about 229 MB here, tens of gigabytes on a real log), and only then filters. Pipeline B lets arrow filter and count, and brings back 4 rows.






Audit it: an early collect()



When an AI writes code for a large dataset, read the pipeline from the top and find the first of collect(), as.data.frame(), as_tibble(), or compute(). Everything after that line runs in R’s memory. The goal is to put as many filter(), select(), and summarize() steps as possible before it.
An AI also often “fixes” an error from an unsupported function by moving collect() to the top of the pipeline. That makes the error disappear and the memory problem appear. The correct fix is to shrink first, then collect, then use the function.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
5.7 Shrink, collect, then join
Arrow can join Datasets, but a simpler pattern is often enough: aggregate in arrow, collect() the small result, and join it to a small in-memory table.

views |>
  count(title) |>
  collect() |>
  left_join(distinct(movies, title, .keep_all = TRUE), by = "title") |>
  summarize(views = sum(n), .by = genre) |>
  arrange(desc(views))

#> # A tibble: 11 x 2
#>    genre                       views
#>    <chr>                       <int>
#>  1 Drama                     1969777
#>  2 Action & Adventure         552152
#>  3 Comedy                     484538
#>  4 Mystery & Suspense         463740
#>  5 Other                      143936
#>  6 Horror                      97385
#>  7 Documentary                 71936
#>  8 Science Fiction & Fantasy   70663
#>  9 Animation                   64769
#> 10 Musical & Performing Arts   47910
#> 11 Art House & International   33194
Four million rows were reduced to one row per title (646) before the join. Notice distinct(movies, title, .keep_all = TRUE): four titles appear twice in movies.csv. Without it, the join would have duplicated their view counts (see Section 3).

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 5.8 Not every R function runs in arrow
text:
5.8 Not every R function runs in arrow
Arrow translates many dplyr verbs and many common functions (arithmetic, comparisons, string functions, date functions, n_distinct(), mean(), and more). A function written by you, or from a package arrow does not know, cannot be translated. The error message names the problem.
What to do:

Run as much as possible in arrow (filter, select, group, summarize).
collect() the small result.
Use the full R function on the result.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 5.9 read_parquet() vs open_dataset(), and writing Parquet
text:
5.9 read_parquet() vs open_dataset(), and writing Parquet

write_parquet(movies, "data/movies.parquet") # write a tibble to Parquet
movies_pq <- read_parquet("data/movies.parquet") # reads ALL rows into memory
views <- open_dataset("data/views.parquet") # lazy: nothing loaded

Use read_parquet() when the file easily fits in memory and you want a tibble. Use open_dataset() when the data is large, or when it is split into many files.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 5.10 A big-data checklist for AI-written code
text:
5.10 A big-data checklist for AI-written code






Check these before running AI-written code on large data




Filter and select first. Fewer rows, fewer columns.
collect() last. After the data is small.
Check the shape. How many rows came back? Is it what you expected?
Check the memory. Watch the Environment pane, or use object.size() on the result.
Check the types. Parquet keeps types; a CSV read guesses them.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
7.1 Many-to-many joins
If a key repeats on both sides, every pair of matching rows is returned, and rows multiply. dplyr warns about an “unexpected many-to-many relationship”. Only set relationship = "many-to-many" when that is exactly what you intend.

title: Session 2 Handout: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
section: 8.1 reframe(): a summary that returns several rows per group
text:
8.1 reframe(): a summary that returns several rows per group
summarize() expects one row per group. When a function returns several values (such as quantiles), use reframe().

movies |>
  reframe(
    quantile = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
    runtime = quantile(runtime, quantile, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = title_type
  )

#> # A tibble: 9 x 3
#>   title_type   quantile runtime
#>   <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Feature Film     0.25      93
#> 2 Feature Film     0.5      104
#> 3 Feature Film     0.75     116
#> 4 Documentary      0.25      86
#> 5 Documentary      0.5       92
#> 6 Documentary      0.75     100
#> # i 3 more rows

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
The slides move fast and are built for discussion. This handout is the slow, complete version: read it before class if you like, and return to it when you are auditing code.
Every section follows the same pattern: a short explanation, code you can run, and Audit it boxes that show a mistake an AI assistant (or a human) could easily make.






The Audit Loop




Read the code.
Run it.
Restate it in plain English. If you cannot say what a line does, you cannot vouch for it.
Refine it or Reject it.



Setup for the examples. Choose a directory to work from inside of Positron and create a data folder in that directory. Every example uses movies.csv (651 movies, 32 columns). Download it here and put it in the data folder you created. The setup code for this handout is below:

library(tidyverse)
movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv")

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
4.1 The types you will meet



Type
Example
class()

3.5, 72
"numeric"


integer
5L
"integer"


character
"Drama"
"character"

TRUE, FALSE
"logical"




class(72)

#> [1] "numeric"

class(5L)

class("Drama")

class(TRUE)

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
4.2 Coercion: when types are mixed
A vector holds one type, so R converts everything to the “most flexible” type present. The order is:
logical < integer < numeric < character

c(TRUE, 2L) # logical -> integer

#> [1] 1 2

c(TRUE, 2L, 3.1) # -> numeric

#> [1] 1.0 2.0 3.1

c(TRUE, 2L, 3.1, "a") # -> character

#> [1] "TRUE" "2"    "3.1"  "a"


You can also convert on purpose with as.numeric(), as.character(), as.logical(), as.integer().






Key idea



A vector holds exactly one type, and R converts silently to make that true. After reading or converting data, always check the types.








Audit it: converting messy text to numbers



as.numeric() quietly turns anything it cannot read into NA. Real data is full of text such as "159.8 lbs".

as.numeric(c("72", "159.8 lbs", "kg"))

#> Warning: NAs introduced by coercion


#> [1] 72 NA NA


R prints a warning, but only once and easily ignored in a long script. After any conversion, count the new NAs: sum(is.na(x)). You will do this with real wearable data in the cleaning sessions.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
4.3 Recycling
When vectors of different lengths are combined, the shorter one is recycled. This is fine for a single number and dangerous otherwise.

c(1, 2, 3, 4) + 10 # 10 is recycled: intended

#> [1] 11 12 13 14

c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20) # recycled in a pattern: legal, rarely intended

#> [1] 11 22 13 24



1:3 + 1:2 # lengths don't divide evenly: R warns

#> Warning in 1:3 + 1:2: longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length


#> [1] 2 4 4

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
4.4 Logical vectors: yes/no questions
Comparisons produce logical vectors. Combine them with & (and), | (or), and ! (not).

scores > 70

#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

scores > 70 & scores < 90

#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

!(scores > 70)

#> [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE


Because TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, you can count and take proportions:

sum(scores > 70) # how many

#> [1] 3

mean(scores > 70) # what fraction

#> [1] 0.75

any(scores > 90) # is at least one TRUE?

#> [1] TRUE

all(scores > 60) # are all TRUE?

#> [1] TRUE


%in% asks whether each value appears anywhere in a set. Compare it with ==:

genres <- c("Drama", "Comedy", "Horror")
genres == "Comedy"

#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE

genres %in% c("Drama", "Horror")

#> [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE








Key idea



Comparisons make logical vectors, and logical vectors can be counted (sum), turned into proportions (mean), and used to select (x[condition]). Most of filter() is this idea applied to a column.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
6.1 Finding and counting NAs
NA == NA is NA, so you cannot test for missing values with ==. Use is.na().

x <- c(4, 8, NA, 2)
is.na(x)

#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

sum(is.na(x)) # how many are missing

#> [1] 1

mean(is.na(x)) # what fraction

#> [1] 0.25

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
6.2 Summaries with missing values

mean(x) # the unknown spreads

#> [1] NA

mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) # remove NAs first

#> [1] 4.666667








na.rm = TRUE is a decision, not a fix



Using na.rm = TRUE means “compute this on the cases where I happen to know the value”. That is only reasonable if the missing cases are not systematically different from the observed ones. In real data they often are. For example, if a smartwatch drops readings more often for certain users, ignoring missing readings quietly changes whose data you are analyzing. Always ask: who is missing, and why?








Audit it: NA inside a logical subset




x[x > 5]

#> [1]  8 NA


The result contains an NA row for the unknown. Applying the same idea to a data frame with filter() behaves differently (it drops those rows), which is also a quiet change. See Section 10.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
7.1 Looking at a data frame

dim(movies) # rows, columns

#> [1] 651  32

nrow(movies)

#> [1] 651

names(movies)[1:6]

#> [1] "title"       "title_type"  "genre"       "runtime"     "mpaa_rating" "studio"


glimpse() shows every column, its type, and the first values. Make it your first move on any new table.

movies |> select(title:mpaa_rating) |> glimpse()

#> Rows: 651
#> Columns: 5
#> $ title       <chr> "Filly Brown", "The Dish", "Waiting for Guffman", "The Age of Innoce…
#> $ title_type  <chr> "Feature Film", "Feature Film", "Feature Film", "Feature Film", "Fea…
#> $ genre       <chr> "Drama", "Drama", "Comedy", "Drama", "Horror", "Documentary", "Drama…
#> $ runtime     <dbl> 80, 101, 84, 139, 90, 78, 142, 93, 88, 119, 127, 108, 110, 100, 111,…
#> $ mpaa_rating <chr> "R", "PG-13", "R", "PG", "R", "Unrated", "PG-13", "R", "Unrated", "U…


summary() gives quick numeric summaries, including how many NAs each column has:

summary(movies$runtime)

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#>    39.0    92.0   103.0   105.8   115.8   267.0       1








Key idea



A data frame is a list of equal-length vectors, so each column is a vector and every vector rule above applies to it.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
10.1 select(): choose columns

movies |> select(title, genre, imdb_rating)

#> # A tibble: 651 × 3
#>   title                genre       imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                <chr>             <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown          Drama               5.5
#> 2 The Dish             Drama               7.3
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman  Comedy              7.6
#> 4 The Age of Innocence Drama               7.2
#> 5 Malevolence          Horror              5.1
#> 6 Old Partner          Documentary         7.8
#> # ℹ 645 more rows


Selection helpers save typing:

movies |> select(title, ends_with("score"))

#> # A tibble: 651 × 3
#>   title                critics_score audience_score
#>   <chr>                        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown                     45             73
#> 2 The Dish                        96             81
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman             91             91
#> 4 The Age of Innocence            80             76
#> 5 Malevolence                     33             27
#> 6 Old Partner                     91             86
#> # ℹ 645 more rows

movies |> select(title, starts_with("thtr"))

#> # A tibble: 651 × 4
#>   title                thtr_rel_year thtr_rel_month thtr_rel_day
#>   <chr>                        <dbl>          <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown                   2013              4           19
#> 2 The Dish                      2001              3           14
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman           1996              8           21
#> 4 The Age of Innocence          1993             10            1
#> 5 Malevolence                   2004              9           10
#> 6 Old Partner                   2009              1           15
#> # ℹ 645 more rows

movies |> select(where(is.numeric)) |> ncol() # how many numeric columns

#> [1] 11

movies |> select(-starts_with("dvd"), -ends_with("url")) |> ncol()

#> [1] 27


Other helpers: contains(), matches() (regular expression), everything(), last_col(). Rename with rename(new = old), and use pull() to extract one column as a vector:

movies |> rename(rating = imdb_rating) |> select(title, rating)

#> # A tibble: 651 × 2
#>   title                rating
#>   <chr>                 <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown             5.5
#> 2 The Dish                7.3
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman     7.6
#> 4 The Age of Innocence    7.2
#> 5 Malevolence             5.1
#> 6 Old Partner             7.8
#> # ℹ 645 more rows

movies |> pull(title) |> head(3)

#> [1] "Filly Brown"         "The Dish"            "Waiting for Guffman"

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
10.2 filter(): keep rows
filter() keeps rows where the condition is TRUE. Several conditions separated by commas mean and.

movies |>
  filter(genre == "Drama", imdb_rating > 8) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating)

#> # A tibble: 8 × 2
#>   title                  imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                        <dbl>
#> 1 Warrior                        8.2
#> 2 V for Vendetta                 8.2
#> 3 The Help                       8.1
#> 4 Good Will Hunting              8.3
#> 5 The Prestige                   8.5
#> 6 No Country for Old Men         8.1
#> # ℹ 2 more rows


More tools: | (or), %in% (membership), between() (inclusive range), and is.na().

movies |> filter(genre %in% c("Drama", "Comedy")) |> nrow()

#> [1] 392

movies |> filter(between(imdb_rating, 7, 8)) |> nrow()

#> [1] 226

movies |> filter(is.na(runtime)) |> select(title, runtime)

#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   title              runtime
#>   <chr>                <dbl>
#> 1 The End of America      NA








Audit it: == against a vector



== compares position by position and recycles the shorter vector. It does not mean “equal to either”.

movies |> filter(genre == c("Drama", "Comedy")) |> nrow() # wrong

#> [1] 191

movies |> filter(genre %in% c("Drama", "Comedy")) |> nrow() # right

#> [1] 392


R prints a warning about lengths in your console. Warnings are clues.








Audit it: comparing with NA



Anything compared with NA is NA, and filter() drops rows where the condition is not TRUE.

movies |> filter(dvd_rel_year != NA) |> nrow() # wrong: zero rows

#> [1] 0

movies |> filter(!is.na(dvd_rel_year)) |> nrow() # right

#> [1] 643










Audit it: filter() silently drops NA rows




nrow(movies)

#> [1] 651

movies |> filter(runtime > 0) |> nrow() # every runtime is positive, but one row vanished

#> [1] 650

movies |> filter(runtime > 0 | is.na(runtime)) |> nrow() # keep unknowns on purpose

#> [1] 651


Any time a row count changes unexpectedly, ask where the rows went. Row-count checks before and after each step are a core habit.








Audit it: and/or precedence



& is evaluated before |, like multiplication before addition. Use parentheses.

movies |>
  filter(genre == "Drama" | genre == "Comedy" & imdb_rating > 8) |>
  nrow()

#> [1] 306

movies |>
  filter((genre == "Drama" | genre == "Comedy") & imdb_rating > 8) |>
  nrow()

#> [1] 9










Audit it: typos and case give zero rows, not errors



Text comparison is exact and case-sensitive.

movies |> filter(genre == "drama") |> nrow()

#> [1] 0

movies |> filter(genre == "Drama") |> nrow()

#> [1] 305


A result with zero rows is a clue that a category name is wrong. Check the real values first with distinct(genre).








Audit it: = instead of ==




movies |> filter(genre = "Drama")

#> Error in `filter()`:
#> ! We detected a named input.
#> ℹ This usually means that you've used `=` instead of `==`.
#> ℹ Did you mean `genre == "Drama"`?


This one is friendly: dplyr stops and explains. Not every mistake is.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
10.3 arrange(): sort rows
Sorting is ascending by default. Use desc() for descending, and add more columns to break ties.

movies |>
  arrange(desc(imdb_rating), title) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating)

#> # A tibble: 651 × 2
#>   title                  imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                        <dbl>
#> 1 The Godfather, Part II         9  
#> 2 Django Unchained               8.5
#> 3 Memento                        8.5
#> 4 Promises                       8.5
#> 5 The Prestige                   8.5
#> 6 Aliens                         8.4
#> # ℹ 645 more rows








Audit it: the most common AI mistake



“Show the 5 highest-rated movies” written as arrange(imdb_rating) |> head(5) returns the five lowest. No error, no warning, a believable table.

movies |> arrange(imdb_rating) |> select(title, imdb_rating) |> head(5)

#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   title             imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                   <dbl>
#> 1 Disaster Movie            1.9
#> 2 Epic Movie                2.3
#> 3 Battlefield Earth         2.4
#> 4 Viva Knievel!             2.7
#> 5 Doogal                    2.8


For top-N questions, slice_max() states the intent directly:

movies |>
  slice_max(imdb_rating, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating)

#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   title                  imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                        <dbl>
#> 1 The Godfather, Part II         9  
#> 2 Promises                       8.5
#> 3 Django Unchained               8.5
#> 4 Memento                        8.5
#> 5 The Prestige                   8.5


with_ties = FALSE returns exactly 5 rows. The default keeps all tied rows, which can return more than you asked for.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
10.4 mutate(): create or change columns
mutate() adds new columns (at the end) or overwrites existing ones.

movies |>
       mutate(runtime_hrs = runtime / 60, decade = thtr_rel_year %/% 10 * 10) |>
       select(title, runtime_hrs, decade)

#> # A tibble: 651 × 3
#>   title                runtime_hrs decade
#>   <chr>                      <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown                 1.33   2010
#> 2 The Dish                    1.68   2000
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman         1.4    1990
#> 4 The Age of Innocence        2.32   1990
#> 5 Malevolence                 1.5    2000
#> 6 Old Partner                 1.3    2000
#> # ℹ 645 more rows


Use if_else() for two outcomes and case_when() for several. They check that the outcomes are the same type, which catches mistakes that base ifelse() hides.

movies |>
  mutate(
    length_class = case_when(
      runtime < 90 ~ "short",
      runtime <= 120 ~ "medium",
      runtime > 120 ~ "long"
    )
  ) |>
  count(length_class)

#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   length_class     n
#>   <chr>        <int>
#> 1 long           120
#> 2 medium         428
#> 3 short          102
#> 4 <NA>             1


Rows that match no condition (here, the movie with an NA runtime) become NA. You can set a default with .default = "unknown".
mutate() keeps all other columns. To keep only the new ones, use mutate(..., .keep = "none"). This replaces the older transmute().






Preview: count()



count(x) counts rows for each value of x. It is shorthand for grouping and summarizing, which is the first topic in Session 2.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
10.5 Other useful verbs

movies |> distinct(mpaa_rating)

#> # A tibble: 6 × 1
#>   mpaa_rating
#>   <chr>      
#> 1 R          
#> 2 PG-13      
#> 3 PG         
#> 4 Unrated    
#> 5 G          
#> 6 NC-17

movies |> slice_head(n = 3) |> select(title)

#> # A tibble: 3 × 1
#>   title              
#>   <chr>              
#> 1 Filly Brown        
#> 2 The Dish           
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman

movies |> slice_max(runtime, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) |> select(title, runtime)

#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   title                                              runtime
#>   <chr>                                                <dbl>
#> 1 Hotel Terminus: The Life and Times of Klaus Barbie     267
#> 2 The Godfather, Part II                                 202
#> 3 Titanic                                                194


For random samples use slice_sample() (this replaces sample_n() and sample_frac()). Set a seed so the sample is reproducible:

set.seed(531)
movies |> slice_sample(n = 3) |> select(title)

#> # A tibble: 3 × 1
#>   title          
#>   <chr>          
#> 1 Mad Dog Time   
#> 2 Blue Valentine 
#> 3 The Big Red One








Audit it: ambiguous questions get confident answers

text:
11.2 for loops
A for loop repeats code once per element.

for (g in c("Drama", "Comedy")) {
  n <- sum(movies$genre == g)
  cat(g, ":", n, "movies\n")
}

#> Drama : 305 movies
#> Comedy : 87 movies

text:
11.3 Functions
A function packages code under a name, with arguments as inputs and the last expression as the returned value.

to_hours <- function(minutes, digits = 1) {
  round(minutes / 60, digits)
}

to_hours(95)

#> [1] 1.6

to_hours(95, digits = 2)

#> [1] 1.58



movies |>
  mutate(runtime_hrs = to_hours(runtime)) |>
  select(title, runtime, runtime_hrs)

#> # A tibble: 651 × 3
#>   title                runtime runtime_hrs
#>   <chr>                  <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown               80         1.3
#> 2 The Dish                 101         1.7
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman       84         1.4
#> 4 The Age of Innocence     139         2.3
#> 5 Malevolence               90         1.5
#> 6 Old Partner               78         1.3
#> # ℹ 645 more rows


How to read an AI-written function: find the arguments and their defaults, find what is returned (the last line or an explicit return()), and look for anything it uses that was not passed in. Functions can silently read variables from outside (Appendix B).

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
A. Matrices and arrays
A matrix is a vector with a dim attribute. It is filled one column at a time.

m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
m

#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    3    5
#> [2,]    2    4    6

m[1, 3] # row 1, column 3

#> [1] 5

m[, 2] # all of column 2

#> [1] 3 4

m[-1, ] # drop row 1

#> [1] 2 4 6


Data frames are not matrices, but df[row, col] indexing works similarly.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
B. Scope and lazy evaluation
Scope. If a function cannot find a variable inside itself, R looks in the surrounding environment. This is convenient and risky: a function can quietly depend on a variable that is not one of its arguments.

cutoff <- 100
is_long <- function(minutes) minutes > cutoff # cutoff is NOT an argument
is_long(120)

#> [1] TRUE

cutoff <- 150
is_long(120) # same call, different answer

#> [1] FALSE


Lazy evaluation. Function arguments are only evaluated when they are used.

f <- function(x) {
  cat("Hello\n")
  x
}
f(stop("this error only fires when x is used"))

#> Hello


#> Error in `f()`:
#> ! this error only fires when x is used


“Hello” prints first: the broken argument is not touched until the function needs it. You will meet the same idea at a larger scale with the arrow package in Session 2, where a query on a huge Parquet file is not run until you ask for the result.

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
text:
C. Vectorization
Most R functions work on whole vectors at once, which is faster and shorter than a loop. But vectorized code can hide edge cases.

p <- c(0.5, 0.5, 0, 0)
-sum(p * log(p)) # entropy: wrong, 0 * log(0) is NaN

#> [1] NaN

p_pos <- p[p > 0]
-sum(p_pos * log(p_pos)) # right: drop the zero-probability cells

#> [1] 0.6931472


NaN means “not a number”. It is a cousin of NA that spreads the same way, and is.na() detects both.
If a function was written for single values and you need it for vectors, Vectorize() can wrap it, but if_else() and case_when() are usually better inside mutate().

title: Session 1 Handout: R Basics and Data Manipulation
section: D. The apply family and purrr
text:
D. The apply family and purrr
apply() and lapply() apply a function across rows, columns, or list elements. The tidyverse version is purrr::map(), with variants that return a specific type (map_dbl() for numbers, map_chr() for text).

nums <- movies |> select(imdb_rating, critics_score, audience_score, runtime)

lapply(nums, mean, na.rm = TRUE) |> unlist() # base R

#>    imdb_rating  critics_score audience_score        runtime 
#>       6.493088      57.688172      62.362519     105.821538

map_dbl(nums, mean, na.rm = TRUE) # purrr: guaranteed numeric result

#>    imdb_rating  critics_score audience_score        runtime 
#>       6.493088      57.688172      62.362519     105.821538


Prefer map_*() over sapply(): sapply() guesses the output type, and a surprise type is a classic silent failure.

E. Old syntax to new syntax








Older code you may see
Use now
Why




x %>% f()
x \|> f()
built into R, no package needed

checks types, safer


tidyr::separate(col, into, sep)

stricter, warns about bad rows

lapply() / sapply()
purrr::map() / map_dbl()
predictable output type

text:
When the file is bigger than your memory
A simulated log of 4 million viewing events:



Format
Size on disk




CSV
239 MB


Parquet
40 MB



read_csv() would pull all 4 million rows into R’s memory (about 229 MB here). A real log could be 400 million.

title: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
What is Parquet?

Columnar: stores each column together, so R reads only the columns you ask for
Typed: dates stay dates, numbers stay numbers
Compressed: much smaller than CSV
Self-describing: the schema lives inside the file

title: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
Setup

install.packages("arrow") # once
library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)

Today’s file: data/views.parquet (download from Canvas). Columns: view_id, title, user_id, country, device, view_date, minutes, completed.

title: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
open_dataset: look without loading

views <- open_dataset("data/views.parquet")

Nothing was loaded. R read only the file’s schema (column names and types).
The query you write next is a recipe. Work happens when you ask for the result.

title: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
Summarize, Combine, and Scale
Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
Interaction 3: where does collect go?

# Pipeline A
views |> collect() |> filter(country == "US") |> count(device)

# Pipeline B
views |> filter(country == "US") |> count(device) |> collect()


Turn to your neighbor (3 min): same answer? Which one would you let an AI run on 400 million rows?


INTERACTION 3 of 3. Give 3 minutes. Answer: both give the same answer. Pipeline A loads ALL rows into memory first (about 229 MB here, tens of GB on a real log), then filters. Pipeline B filters and counts inside arrow and brings back 4 rows. Rule: shrink first, collect last.

title: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
The answer
Same result. Very different cost.
A loads every row, then filters. B filters first, then collects 4 rows.


Bug to look for: an early collect(), as.data.frame(), or as_tibble(). It silently pulls the whole dataset into memory.

section: Not every R function runs in arrow
text:
Not every R function runs in arrow
arrow translates many dplyr verbs and functions. A few things it cannot run.
When you see an error that mentions an unsupported function:

collect() only after shrinking the data
Then use the full R function on the small result

Never fix it by moving collect() to the top.

title: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
Big-data checklist for AI code

Filter and select first: fewer rows, fewer columns
collect() last: after the data is small
Check the shape: how many rows came back?
Check the memory: Environment pane, or object.size()

title: Summarize, Combine, and Scale
text:
Three things to remember

Summaries: group on purpose, show n, decide what to do with NA.
Joins: check keys, row counts, and new NAs every time.
Scale: shrink in arrow, collect() last.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
The slides move fast. This handout is the slow, complete version: read it before class, and return to it when you audit a plot.
As in the earlier sessions, Audit it boxes show mistakes that an AI assistant (or a human) could easily make. For plots there is a new kind of mistake: the code runs without error, and the picture is still misleading.






NoteThe Audit Loop, for plots




Read the code.
Run it, and look at the plot with the data in mind.
Restate what the plot claims in plain English.
Refine it or Reject it: axis, sample sizes, order, color, labels.



Setup. Every example uses movies.csv (download). The packages come with tidyverse: ggplot2 (plots), forcats (ordering categories), and scales (axis labels).

library(tidyverse)
movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv")

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
section: 3.1 Build one plot, layer by layer
text:
3.1 Build one plot, layer by layer
Start with the canvas: data and aesthetics only.

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score))








The axes exist because ggplot2 looked at the columns, but nothing is drawn. Add a geom:

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point()








Add a second layer. Both layers inherit x and y from the first line.

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)








geom_smooth() fits a trend. method = "lm" is a straight line. The default (method = "loess") is a flexible curve. se = FALSE hides the uncertainty band; leave it on when you want to show how sure the trend is.
You can also write the data into the pipeline:

movies |>
  ggplot(aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point()







NotePipe, then plus



Inside a pipeline, the pipe |> passes data into ggplot(). After that, layers are joined with +. A common AI mistake is to use |> between layers (or + between data steps).

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
3.2 Mapping vs setting
This is the most important idea in the grammar.

Inside aes(): the property depends on the data. A legend is created.
Outside aes(): one fixed value for every element. No legend.


# Mapped: color depends on a column
ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = title_type))









# Set: every point is the same fixed color, size, and transparency
ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "#6d8d24", size = 2, alpha = 0.5)














WarningAudit it: a color name inside aes()




ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = "blue"))








The points are not blue, and there is a legend entry called “blue”. Inside aes(), "blue" is just a text label for a (single) category, so ggplot2 assigns it the first default palette color. To get blue points, set the color outside aes(): geom_point(color = "blue").

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
3.3 Which aesthetic for which variable?








Aesthetic
Works well for
Notes




x, y (position)
numbers, ordered categories
The most accurate encoding. Use it for what matters most.


color
a few categories, or a continuous gradient
Limit to about 5 categories


fill
the inside of bars, boxes, densities
color is the outline for these


shape
2 to 4 categories
Hard to read for more


size
a number, roughly
Readers compare sizes poorly


alpha
overlap, or a number
Transparency


linetype
a few categories of lines



group
which points belong to the same line
Often needed with geom_line()









TipKey idea



Put the variable that matters most on a position (x or y). Use color and size for secondary variables.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
3.4 Plots are objects
Save a plot in a name and keep adding layers.

p <- ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#6d8d24")

p + labs(title = "Audience scores track IMDB ratings")








Nothing is displayed when you assign (p <- ...). Type p or add layers to see it. This is the best way to try several versions of a plot.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
4.1 One number: histograms and densities

ggplot(movies, aes(x = audience_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#6d8d24", color = "white")








Each bar counts the movies in a bin. binwidth = 5 means a bin spans 5 points. The bin width is a choice that changes the look (see Section 6.3).
A density plot is a smoothed version, and it works well for comparing groups, as long as the fills are see-through:

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, fill = audience_rating)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)








audience_rating is “Upright” (audience score at least 60) or “Spilled” (below 60).

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
4.2 A number across groups: boxplots
A boxplot shows the median (the line), the middle half of the data (the box), and the range with outliers (whiskers and dots).

ggplot(movies, aes(x = audience_score, y = genre)) +
  geom_boxplot()








The categories are in alphabetical order, which carries no meaning. fct_reorder() sorts them by a summary of the number (the median, by default):

ggplot(movies, aes(x = audience_score, y = fct_reorder(genre, audience_score))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(y = NULL)








Putting the long category names on the y axis avoids the overlapping labels you get on a crowded x axis.






TipShow the points too



A boxplot hides group sizes. Adding geom_jitter() on top shows every observation, so a group with 9 movies cannot masquerade as one with 300.

ggplot(movies, aes(x = audience_score, y = fct_reorder(genre, audience_score))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(y = NULL)








outlier.shape = NA hides the boxplot’s own outlier dots, because the jittered points already show them.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
4.3 Counts: geom_bar() vs geom_col()
geom_bar() counts rows for you:

ggplot(movies, aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(genre)))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(y = NULL)








fct_infreq() orders categories by how often they occur, and fct_rev() flips the order so the biggest bar is on top.
If you already have the counts (or any summary) in a column, use geom_col():

genre_counts <- movies |> count(genre)

ggplot(genre_counts, aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(genre, n))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(y = NULL)














WarningAudit it: geom_bar() with a count column




ggplot(genre_counts, aes(x = n, y = genre)) +
  geom_bar()

#> Error in `geom_bar()`:
#> ! Problem while computing stat.
#> i Error occurred in the 1st layer.
#> Caused by error in `setup_params()`:
#> ! `stat_count()` must only have an x or y aesthetic.


geom_bar() counts rows itself, so it refuses a variable already on the count axis. The fix is geom_col() (or geom_bar(stat = "identity"), the older spelling). The wording of the error message varies between versions of ggplot2.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
section: 4.4 Position: stacked, dodged, and filled bars
text:
4.4 Position: stacked, dodged, and filled bars
When bars are split by a second variable, position decides how:

ggplot(movies, aes(y = genre, fill = audience_rating)) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack") +      # the default: totals plus parts
  labs(y = NULL, title = "stack")









ggplot(movies, aes(y = genre, fill = audience_rating)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +      # side by side
  labs(y = NULL, title = "dodge")









ggplot(movies, aes(y = genre, fill = audience_rating)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +       # every bar rescaled to 100%
  labs(x = "proportion", y = NULL, title = "fill")








Use stack for totals, dodge to compare parts directly, and fill to compare shares. fill hides how big each group is, so say so or show n.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
4.5 Two numbers: overplotting
When many points land on top of each other, density is hidden. Three fixes: transparency (alpha), jitter, or smaller points.

ggplot(movies, aes(x = mpaa_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point()








Points at the same rating stack in a single line. geom_jitter() adds a small random shift so they spread out:

ggplot(movies, aes(x = mpaa_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.5)








Jitter changes only the drawing, not the data. Keep height = 0 when the vertical value must stay exact.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
4.7 Facets: small multiples
Facets draw one panel per group, on the same scales. They are usually clearer than 11 colors.

movies |>
  filter(genre %in% c("Drama", "Comedy", "Documentary", "Horror")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ genre)









facet_wrap(~ genre) wraps panels into a grid.
facet_grid(rows = vars(a), cols = vars(b)) makes a grid from two variables.
scales = "free" lets each panel have its own axes. That helps with different ranges, but it makes panels harder to compare, so use it knowingly.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
5.1 Labels

p +
  labs(
    title = "Audience scores track IMDB ratings",
    subtitle = "651 movies released 1970 to 2014",
    x = "IMDB rating (0 to 10)",
    y = "Audience score (0 to 100)",
    caption = "Source: movies.csv (IMDB and Rotten Tomatoes)"
  )








Good labels name the units and the source. Defaults such as imdb_num_votes are for you, not for your reader.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
section: 5.2 Position scales: breaks, limits, labels, logs
text:
5.2 Position scales: breaks, limits, labels, logs
Position scales are named scale_x_*() and scale_y_*().

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_num_votes, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#6d8d24") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "IMDB votes (log scale)", y = "Audience score")








imdb_num_votes is heavily skewed: a few movies have hundreds of thousands of votes. On a log scale equal distances mean equal ratios, which spreads out the crowd. Always say when an axis is logged.
Useful label helpers from the scales package:



Helper
Example result




scales::label_comma()
1,000,000


scales::label_percent()
25% (for a proportion such as 0.25)


scales::label_dollar()
$1,500




movies |>
  count(genre) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = fct_reorder(genre, share))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#6d8d24") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Share of movies", y = NULL)














WarningAudit it: zooming with limits deletes data



ylim(), xlim(), and scale_*_continuous(limits = ...) remove data outside the range before anything is computed. coord_cartesian(xlim = , ylim = ) only zooms the view.

by_rating <- movies |>
  summarize(avg = mean(audience_score), n = n(), .by = mpaa_rating)

ggplot(by_rating, aes(x = mpaa_rating, y = avg)) +
  geom_col() +
  ylim(60, 80)

#> Warning: Removed 6 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_col()`).









The warning says rows were removed. Bars below the limit vanish, and the rest are cut off. Reading a warning like this is part of the audit. If you really need to zoom, use coord_cartesian(), and even then think twice for bars (see Section 6.1).

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
5.3 Color scales
The default palette is fine for exploration, but it is not always readable for everyone. About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of color vision deficiency, and red versus green is the most common confusion.

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score, color = mpaa_rating)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_d()















Scale
Use for




scale_color_viridis_d() / scale_fill_viridis_d()
discrete categories; readable in grayscale and for most color-blind viewers


scale_color_viridis_c()
a continuous variable


scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2")
discrete categories (ColorBrewer palettes)


scale_color_manual(values = c(...))
colors you choose yourself



A manual palette is easiest to control. These eight colors (the Okabe-Ito palette) were designed to be distinguishable by color-blind readers:

okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
               "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000")

movies |>
  filter(genre %in% c("Drama", "Comedy", "Documentary", "Horror")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score, color = genre)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito)














TipFewer colors, used on purpose



The strongest color design is often gray plus one accent: mute everything except the group you want the reader to see (see Section 8).

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
5.4 Legends

p2 + theme(legend.position = "bottom")   # "top", "bottom", "left", "right", "none"
p2 + guides(color = guide_legend(title = "MPAA rating"))
p2 + labs(color = "MPAA rating")          # the simplest way to rename a legend

Remove a legend that adds nothing with legend.position = "none", for example when you have labeled the groups directly or in facet titles.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
5.5 Themes and saving
A theme controls everything that is not data: background, gridlines, fonts.

p +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








theme_minimal(), theme_bw(), and theme_classic() change the whole look. theme() adjusts individual details, for example theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) for tilted labels. Use base_size to scale all text at once.
Save a plot with ggsave(). Set the size and resolution yourself:

ggsave("audience_vs_imdb.png", p, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)

In a Quarto document, set figure size per chunk with #| fig-width: 8 and #| fig-height: 4, and describe the figure for screen readers with #| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of ...".

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
6.1 Truncated bar axes
A bar encodes its value by its length, so the baseline must be zero. Zooming a bar chart makes small differences look large.

ggplot(by_rating, aes(x = mpaa_rating, y = avg)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(50, 80))








Here “Unrated” looks several times taller than “PG-13”, although 78.5 versus 56.7 is a ratio of about 1.4. There are three more problems: the order is alphabetical, nothing shows that NC-17 is the average of only 2 movies, and the label avg means nothing to a reader.
An honest version starts at zero, sorts by value, shows n, and labels the axes:

ggplot(by_rating, aes(x = avg, y = fct_reorder(mpaa_rating, avg))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#6d8d24") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Average audience score (0 to 100)", y = NULL,
       title = "Average audience score by MPAA rating")














NotePoints do not need a zero baseline



The zero-baseline rule is for bars. A dot or line chart encodes value by position, so zooming to the range of the data is fine, as long as the axis labels make it visible.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
6.2 Averages without sizes
A mean of 2 values and a mean of 300 values look identical in a bar. Always show or mention n, as above. For skewed data, a boxplot or the individual points (Section 4.2) say more than a mean.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
6.3 Bin width changes the story

ggplot(movies, aes(x = audience_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, fill = "#6d8d24", color = "white")









ggplot(movies, aes(x = audience_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#6d8d24", color = "white")








Wide bins hide the shape; very narrow bins add noise. Try several widths (or a density plot) before choosing one, and never choose a width because it makes your claim look better.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
6.4 Other things to look for







Problem
What to check




Dual y axes
Two series on separate axes can be made to look correlated by choosing the scales. ggplot2 makes this hard on purpose (sec.axis only supports a transformation of one axis). Be suspicious when an AI produces one.


Too many colors
More than about 5 categories force the reader to match dots to a legend. Facet, or highlight one group.


3D and pie charts
Angles and areas are read poorly. A sorted bar chart is almost always better.


Area and size encodings
Doubling a radius quadruples the area. Prefer position.


Log axes
Is it labeled? Can your reader read it?


Cherry-picked range
Does the x range exclude inconvenient years?


Missing context
Units, date range, source, and sample size









TipChart audit checklist




Axis: do bars start at zero? Is a zoom or log scale stated?
Size: is n visible for averages and proportions?
Order: is the order meaningful, not alphabetical?
Color: few colors, color-blind safe, used for a reason?
Labels: title says something, units, source?
Warnings: did R remove rows or drop values? Read every warning.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
7.1 Distributions: outliers and impossible values

ggplot(movies, aes(x = runtime)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "#6d8d24", color = "white")








A single bar sits far to the right. Find it:

movies |>
  slice_max(runtime, n = 3) |>
  select(title, runtime, genre)

#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>   title                                              runtime genre             
#>   <chr>                                                <dbl> <chr>             
#> 1 Hotel Terminus: The Life and Times of Klaus Barbie     267 Documentary       
#> 2 The Godfather, Part II                                 202 Mystery & Suspense
#> 3 Titanic                                                194 Drama


A 267-minute documentary (the 1988 film Hotel Terminus) is unusual but real. A plot flags a value; you decide whether it is an error, an outlier worth keeping, or a different kind of observation. Deleting it just because the plot looks better would be its own kind of dishonesty.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
section: 7.2 Missing data: how much, and where?

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
7.3 Missing for whom? Subgroup comparison
Is missingness spread evenly across groups?

movies |>
  summarize(n = n(), n_no_dvd = sum(is.na(dvd_rel_year)),
            pct_no_dvd = mean(is.na(dvd_rel_year)), .by = title_type)

#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   title_type       n n_no_dvd pct_no_dvd
#>   <chr>        <int>    <int>      <dbl>
#> 1 Feature Film   591        6     0.0102
#> 2 Documentary     55        2     0.0364
#> 3 TV Movie         5        0     0



movies |>
  summarize(pct_no_dvd = mean(is.na(dvd_rel_year)), n = n(), .by = title_type) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pct_no_dvd, y = title_type)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#6d8d24") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 0.2)) +
  labs(x = "Share with no DVD release year", y = NULL)








With only 5 TV movies (and none missing), 55 documentaries (2 missing), and 591 feature films (6 missing), the percentages are small and based on very few cases. Always read a percentage together with its n.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
section: 7.4 Relationships: does the data agree with itself?
text:
7.4 Relationships: does the data agree with itself?
Two columns that should agree can be checked with a scatter plot and a reference line:

ggplot(movies, aes(x = critics_score, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#f68b1f") +
  labs(x = "Critics score", y = "Audience score")








Points above the orange line are movies audiences rated higher than critics did. Most of the cloud sits above or near it, so audiences are on average a little more generous. Unexpected structure, such as a hard edge or a vertical stripe, would suggest a data entry or coding issue.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
8.1 An example, step by step
The question: do critics and audiences rate genres differently? First the numbers:

gap <- movies |>
  summarize(critics = mean(critics_score), audience = mean(audience_score), .by = genre) |>
  mutate(gap = audience - critics)

gap |> arrange(desc(gap))

#> # A tibble: 11 x 4
#>   genre                     critics audience   gap
#>   <chr>                       <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Art House & International    51.6     64   12.4 
#> 2 Action & Adventure           41.4     53.8 12.4 
#> 3 Animation                    50.2     62.4 12.2 
#> 4 Comedy                       40.9     52.5 11.6 
#> 5 Musical & Performing Arts    76.7     80.2  3.5 
#> 6 Drama                        62.2     65.3  3.13
#> # i 5 more rows


Version 1: the default. It shows the data, but the reader has to do all the work.

gap |>
  pivot_longer(c(critics, audience), names_to = "source", values_to = "score") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = score, y = genre, color = source)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)








Version 2: sort by the finding. Connect each pair with a segment so the gap is the visible object.

ggplot(gap, aes(y = fct_reorder(genre, gap))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = critics, xend = audience, yend = genre), color = "grey75", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = critics), color = "grey40", size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = audience), color = "#213921", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Average score", y = NULL)








Version 3: highlight the finding and say it in the title.

gap |>
  mutate(big = gap > 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = fct_reorder(genre, gap))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = critics, xend = audience, yend = genre, color = big),
               linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = critics), color = "grey40", size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = audience), color = "#213921", size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey80", "#f68b1f"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Critics score four genres about 12 points below audiences",
       subtitle = "Grey dot: critics. Dark green dot: audience. Gaps over 10 points in orange.",
       x = "Average score (0 to 100)", y = NULL,
       caption = "Source: movies.csv, 651 movies (IMDB and Rotten Tomatoes)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








What changed: the title states the finding, one color carries the message, the order follows the gap, and the legend became a one-line subtitle. No data was altered.






TipChecklist for a plot that makes a point




Title = finding, in a sentence (not “Critics vs audience by genre”).
One highlight; mute everything else.
Sort by what matters.
Label directly when you can, instead of using a legend.
Remove clutter: extra gridlines, borders, redundant legends.
Context: units, source, and the sample size.
Accessibility: color-blind safe, large enough text, alt text.









WarningAudit it: a headline the data cannot support



An AI may write a confident title such as “Critics hate comedies.” The plot shows an average difference of about 12 points across 87 comedies. It does not show that critics “hate” anything, or why they differ. Check that your title claims no more than the plot shows. Be careful with causal words (because, drives, leads to) in a title.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
8.2 Annotations and direct labels
annotate() adds a note at a position in data coordinates. geom_text() labels points from a column.

movies |>
  count(thtr_rel_year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = thtr_rel_year, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = ~ slice_max(.x, n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE), color = "#f68b1f", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2006, y = 35.5, label = "Peak: 33 movies in 2006 (and 2007)", hjust = 1) +
  labs(title = "Movies in the sample per release year", x = NULL, y = "Movies")








The highlighted point uses a function as the data for one layer (data = ~ slice_max(.x, n, n = 1)), so the label stays correct if the data changes. For many labels that would overlap, the ggrepel package (Appendix B) places them for you.

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +

Distribution of one number

ggplot(movies, aes(x = audience_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#6d8d24", color = "white")








Each bar counts the movies in a 5-point bin.

section: A plot can lie without a bug
text:
A plot can lie without a bug
Code that runs is not code that is honest.
An AI will happily:

zoom the axis to make a small difference look huge
show an average without saying how many rows are behind it
sort categories alphabetically instead of meaningfully

title: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
Interaction 2: audit this AI plot

ggplot(by_rating, aes(x = mpaa_rating, y = avg)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(50, 80))









Neighbor (3 min): list every problem you can find.


INTERACTION 2 of 3. The AI was asked: “Plot the average audience score by rating.” Give 3 minutes. Answers on the next slide. Problems: (1) the y axis starts at 50, so bar heights are not proportional to the values (bars encode value by length); (2) NC-17 is the average of only 2 movies, and no n is shown; (3) categories are in alphabetical order, not sorted by the value; (4) no title or axis labels (y is “avg”); (5) a bar chart of averages hides the spread.

title: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
The problems

Truncated axis: bars start at 50, so the length no longer matches the value

  labs(x = "Average audience score", y = NULL)

A plot is a diagnostic and a message: find the problem, then state the finding.

text:
6.5 Prompting for a plot
An AI assistant gives you what you ask for, so a vague prompt gets a plot that runs but may not be honest. A good plot prompt names five things:

Data: the data frame and the exact column names (the AI cannot see your data unless you tell it).
Message: what the reader should see.
Form: the geom, and the order of the categories.
Honesty rules: a zero baseline for bars, n shown, labels with units, color-blind safe colors.
Output: “Return only ggplot2 code” (so you can paste and run it).









Prompt




Weak
“Make a bar chart of average audience score by rating.”


Strong
“Using the data frame by_rating (columns mpaa_rating, avg, n), make a horizontal bar chart of avg, sorted from high to low. Start the axis at 0 and write n = at the end of each bar. Label the axis with units and give the plot a title that states the finding. Return only ggplot2 code.”



The weak prompt tends to produce the truncated, alphabetical, unlabeled chart from Section 6.1. The strong prompt produces something close to the honest version.






TipDescribe the problem in your own words, not just the fix



When a result is wrong, say what is wrong and what you want: “The bars start at 50, which exaggerates the differences. Start the axis at 0.” Paste the exact error message or warning when there is one, and tell the AI which package versions you use if the code fails.

title: Session 3 Handout: Plots That Tell the Truth
text:
6.6 Assessing what comes back
Whatever the AI returns, apply the Audit Loop:

Read the code. Is every column name one that exists? Are mappings inside aes() and fixed settings outside?
Run it, and read every warning and error.
Restate: what does the plot claim, and what does its title claim? Are those the same?
Refine with a more specific prompt, or Reject the result.

Try it. An AI was asked, “Show how critics and audiences rate genres differently, with a title,” and returned this:

gap <- movies |>
  summarize(critics = mean(critics_score), audience = mean(audience_score), .by = genre) |>
  mutate(gap = audience - critics)

gap |>
  ggplot(aes(x = genre, y = gap, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Audiences always rate movies higher than critics")

#> Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
#> i Please use `linewidth` instead.















WarningAudit it: code that runs, with a claim that does not hold




Code: size for lines is deprecated (use linewidth), and group = 1 forces one line through unrelated categories.
Plot: a line implies a trend from one genre to the next, but genres have no order. They are alphabetical, the labels collide, and the axis label is the column name gap. It also plots only the difference, so you cannot see either score.
Title: “always” is false. For Documentary the gap is about -3.6 (critics rate higher), and for several genres it is near zero.



Section 8.1 shows the kind of plot a good prompt should lead to.
