text:
Task 1: code it
An AI was asked: “Make the points blue.” It wrote:

ggplot(movies, aes(x = imdb_rating, y = audience_score)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = "blue"))


Code it (4 min). Run it. Are the points blue? Fix it, then add a straight trend line (no band) and axis labels with units.


TASK 1 of 3 (CODE IT). Give 4 minutes; walk the room. Expected fix: move color outside aes(), add geom_smooth(method = “lm”, se = FALSE), add labs(x = “IMDB rating (0 to 10)”, y = “Audience score (0 to 100)”). Answer: the points are NOT blue. They are the default first palette color (a salmon red), and there is a legend entry labeled “blue”. Inside aes(), “blue” is just the text of a category, so ggplot2 maps it to a color like any other label. Common stuck points: forgetting the + at the end of a line, putting color = “blue” still inside aes(), method = lm without quotes. Four kinds of “nothing”



Looks like
Is it missing?




NA
yes: R’s missing value


NaN
yes: not a number (0/0)


"", "n/a", "NULL"
text pretending to be a value


-999, -1, 9999
a sentinel: a number that means “no data”



NULL is different: it means “no object” and cannot sit inside a data frame column.

vit_na |>
  mutate(
    hr_flag = case_when(
      is.na(hr) ~ "missing",
      between(hr, 30, 220) ~ "ok",
      .default = "impossible"
    )
  ) |>
  count(hr_flag)

#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   hr_flag        n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 impossible    12
#> 2 missing       29
#> 3 ok           959


Keep the row. Keep the flag. A later step decides what to do.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Task 1: code it
vitals has sentinels (-999, -1) and impossible heart rates (0, 300).

Code it (5 min). 1. Turn the sentinels into NA. 2. Flag heart rates outside 30 to 220 as "impossible". 3. Compare the mean heart rate before and after, using only "ok" rows.


TASK 1 of 3 (CODE IT). Give 5 minutes; walk the room. Expected: vit <- vitals |> mutate(hr = na_if(hr, -999), steps = na_if(steps, -1), hr_flag = case_when(is.na(hr) ~ “missing”, between(hr, 30, 220) ~ “ok”, .default = “impossible”)); then mean(vitals$hr) is 41.2 (raw) and vit |> filter(hr_flag == “ok”) |> summarize(mean(hr)) is about 72. Counts: 29 missing (30 sentinels, one of which was overwritten by another planted value), 12 impossible (8 zeros and 4 values of 300), 959 ok. Steps: 25 sentinels. Common stuck points: case_when order (the NA check must come first, or between(NA) returns NA and the row falls to .default), using == instead of na_if, deleting rows instead of flagging them, mean() returning NA because the NAs were not dropped (na.rm = TRUE, and say so). Early finishers: add a flag for steps above 60000 and count it. Land the point: three different problems share one column: a sentinel, an impossible value, and a plausible one. Each needs a different decision, which is why we flag instead of overwrite.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
The answer

c(raw = mean(vitals$hr), clean = mean(hr_ok$hr))

#>      raw    clean 
#> 41.20000 71.91971

count(vit, hr_flag)

#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   hr_flag        n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 impossible    12
#> 2 missing       29
#> 3 ok           959




Bug: the raw mean was off by 30 bpm, from sentinels alone.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: z-scores: how far from the rest?
text:
z-scores: how far from the rest?
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\]
For roughly bell-shaped data, about 0.3% of values are beyond \(|z| > 3\).

nrow(hr_ok)

#> [1] 959

c(expected = round(0.0027 * nrow(hr_ok), 1), found = sum(abs(zs(hr_ok$hr)) > 3))

#> expected    found 
#>      2.6      5.0


Close to what a bell curve gives: nothing alarming here.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
The IQR rule
A value is “unusual” if it is beyond 1.5 x IQR from the quartiles. This is the rule a boxplot uses.

ggplot(steps_ok, aes(x = steps)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#cfd82d", outlier.color = "#f68b1f")

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: z or IQR? It depends on the shape
text:
z or IQR? It depends on the shape

tibble(
       variable = c("hr (bell-shaped)", "steps (skewed)"),
       z_beyond_3 = c(
              sum(abs(zs(hr_ok$hr)) > 3),
              sum(abs(zs(steps_ok$steps)) > 3)
       ),
       iqr_rule = c(sum(iqr_flag(hr_ok$hr)), sum(iqr_flag(steps_ok$steps))),
       n = c(nrow(hr_ok), nrow(steps_ok))
)

#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>   variable         z_beyond_3 iqr_rule     n
#>   <chr>                 <int>    <int> <int>
#> 1 hr (bell-shaped)          5        8   959
#> 2 steps (skewed)           14       32   975


Skewed data flags many “outliers” on the long tail. Rare is not wrong.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Look in context

Impossible? A bound says so: flag as an error.
Plausible but extreme? Keep it: it may be your most interesting data.
Repeated? The same odd value many times: look for a code, not a person.


Outliers are questions, not verdicts. Flag, look, document.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Odd only in combination

hw |> filter(id == 501) |> select(h, w, zh, zw, bmi, zb)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>       h     w    zh    zw   bmi    zb
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   190    45  2.17 -2.07  12.5 -3.73


Height and weight each look normal: \(|z| < 3\). But BMI is 12.5, far below normal.

A derived feature can catch what each column alone cannot.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Mahalanobis distance (FLEX)

hw |> filter(md > qchisq(.999, 2)) |> select(id, h, w, md)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>      id     h     w    md
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   501   190    45  27.7


One distance for several variables at once. It accounts for how they move together. Cutoff: \(\chi^2_2\) at 99.9%, about 13.8.

FLEX: skip if behind (saves about 1.5 min). Assumes roughly multivariate normal data. It flags the one planted case (height 190, weight 45), which no single-variable z-score does.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Dimensions of data quality



Dimension
The question




Validity
Does it follow the rules?


Accuracy
Is it close to the truth?


Consistency
Does it agree with itself and other tables?


Uniformity
Same units, same format?


Completeness
Is everything we need here?



A value can be valid and still wrong: 120 is a valid heart rate that may be false.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: Validity rules you can write as code
text:
Validity rules you can write as code



Rule type
Example




Data type
age is numeric


Range
age between 0 and 120


Mandatory
id is never NA


Unique
id appears once


Set membership
device is watch, band, or ring


Pattern
zip is exactly 5 digits


Cross-field
end is not before start

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Rules become counts

users |>
  summarize(
    id_missing = sum(is.na(id)),
    age_range = sum(!between(age, 0, 120), na.rm = TRUE),
    device_set = sum(!device %in% c("watch", "band", "ring")),
    zip_pattern = sum(!str_detect(zip, "^\\d{5}$"), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "rule", values_to = "failing")

#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   rule        failing
#>   <chr>         <int>
#> 1 id_missing        1
#> 2 age_range         2
#> 3 device_set        2
#> 4 zip_pattern       2


A table of failing counts is a report you can rerun on every new file.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Task 2: prompt it
Rules for users (from the data dictionary):
id: never missing, unique · age: 0 to 120 · device: watch, band, ring · zip: 5 digits · end not before start

Prompt it (6 min). 1. Count by hand the failing rows per rule. 2. Prompt your AI for check_rules(df): one row per rule, with the failing count. It must not change the data. 3. Run it. Do your counts match?


TASK 2 of 3 (PROMPT IT). Give 6 minutes: about 2 for the hand count, 2 for prompting, 2 for running and comparing. Expected failing counts (users has 10 rows): id missing 1; id duplicated 1 (the second 3); age out of range 2 (151 and -2; the NA age is not out of range, it is missing); device not in set 2 (“Watch” with a capital, and “phone”); zip not 5 digits 2 (“9720” and “97201-1234”; the NA zip is missing, not malformed); end before start 4. A good prompt: pastes the dictionary rules as text, says the function takes a data frame and returns a tibble with columns rule and n_failing, forbids modifying or dropping rows, says to handle NA explicitly (and say how), and asks for dplyr only. Where it goes wrong: the AI counts NA as failing (or as passing) without saying so; counts BOTH copies of a duplicate id (2 instead of 1) or flags the first one; uses a case-insensitive device check so “Watch” passes; returns the cleaned data instead of the report; or pulls in a package nobody has. The hand count exists to catch exactly these. Land the point: when the counts differ, the DISAGREEMENT is the finding. Decide which count is right, then write that decision into the prompt.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
The answer

users |>
  summarize(
    id_missing = sum(is.na(id)),
    id_duplicated = sum(duplicated(id[!is.na(id)])),
    age_range = sum(!between(age, 0, 120), na.rm = TRUE),
    device_set = sum(!device %in% c("watch", "band", "ring")),
    zip_pattern = sum(!str_detect(zip, "^\\d{5}$"), na.rm = TRUE),
    end_early = sum(end < start)
  )

#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   id_missing id_duplicated age_range device_set zip_pattern end_early
#>        <int>         <int>     <int>      <int>       <int>     <int>
#> 1          1             1         2          2           2         4

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Decisions hidden in the counts

NA age: not out of range. It is missing, a different problem
Duplicated id: count the extra copies, or both?
"Watch": invalid by the rule. Case-fold first, or flag it?
97201-1234: malformed, or a valid ZIP+4?


The rule table is code and documentation. Write the decision down.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Why is it missing?








Type
Meaning
Example




Structural
cannot exist
“last pregnancy date” for a man


MCAR
unrelated to anything
a random sync failure


MAR
related to other columns
old devices drop steps


MNAR
related to the missing value itself
heart rate dropped when it is high



Real data is rarely MCAR. The mechanism decides what is safe to do.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: Diagnose: is missingness the same everywhere?
text:
Diagnose: is missingness the same everywhere?

steps_sim |>
  summarize(missing = mean(is.na(steps)), n = n(), .by = device)

#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   device missing     n
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1 new     0.0798  1203
#> 2 legacy  0.512    797


Legacy devices lose 51% of steps, new devices 8%. That is not random.

You can describe this pattern. You cannot prove the cause from the file.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: Drop the rows? Look at who is left
text:
Drop the rows? Look at who is left

steps_sim |>
  summarize(
    all_rows = mean(device == "legacy"),
    complete_rows = mean(device[!is.na(steps)] == "legacy")
  )

#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   all_rows complete_rows
#>      <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1    0.398         0.260


Legacy devices were 40% of users, but only 26% of complete rows.


Bug: dropping rows with NA removes legacy users first. The model then learns mostly from new-device users.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
MNAR leaves no trace
If heart rate goes missing because it was high, no other column shows it.

Only context can raise the suspicion: how does the sensor behave when the wearer is exercising?

What you can do: ask the source, compare with another source, or test how much the answer changes under different assumptions (a sensitivity analysis).

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: Options, and the rule of thumb
text:
Options, and the rule of thumb







Option
When




Drop rows
few missing (under about 5 to 10%) and MCAR


Drop the variable
mostly missing, little value


Impute
MAR, and the variable is a predictor


Declare unusable
too much missing, or MNAR with no way to check



Never impute the label or the outcome you are trying to predict.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Mean imputation: the tempting one

mean_imp <- steps_sim |>
  mutate(steps = if_else(is.na(steps), mean(steps, na.rm = TRUE), steps))

c(true_sd = sd(steps_sim$steps_true), after_mean_imp = sd(mean_imp$steps))

#>        true_sd after_mean_imp 
#>       2564.128       2193.206


The mean stays put. The spread shrinks, because one value now fills 25% of the column.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: What it does to the shape
text:
What it does to the shape

bind_rows(
        truth = steps_sim |> transmute(steps = steps_true),
        `mean imputed` = mean_imp |> select(steps),
        .id = "version"
) |>
        ggplot(aes(x = steps, fill = version)) +
        geom_density(alpha = 0.5, color = NA) +
        scale_fill_manual(values = c("#6d8d24", "#f68b1f"), name = NULL)

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Multiple imputation with mice

library(mice)
dat <- steps_sim |>
  select(steps, device, age) |>
  mutate(device = factor(device))
imp <- mice(
  dat,
  m = 5,
  method = "pmm",
  donors = 20,
  printFlag = FALSE,
  seed = 531
)


m = 5: five completed datasets, to carry the uncertainty
pmm: fill each hole with an observed value from a similar row
Analyze each dataset, then pool

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Judge it by the distribution

stats <- \(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))
pooled <- sapply(1:5, \(i) stats(complete(imp, i)$steps))

rbind(
      truth = stats(steps_sim$steps_true),
      `drop rows` = stats(na.omit(steps_sim$steps)),
      `mean imputed` = stats(mean_imp$steps),
      `mice (pooled)` = rowMeans(pooled)
) |>
      round()

#>               mean   sd
#> truth         7419 2564
#> drop rows     7791 2536
#> mean imputed  7791 2193
#> mice (pooled) 7404 2604



Real data has no truth column. There you compare distributions and group means before and after, never single imputed values.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Task 3: assess it

Assess it (5 min). Run it. Compare with steps_true and with the group means by device. Read, Run, Restate.


Is the claim “no bias” true? Check two things.
What happened to the spread?
What does it do to legacy users?
What would you ask for instead?


TASK 3 of 3 (ASSESS IT). Give 5 minutes. Findings: (1) The mean is unchanged BY CONSTRUCTION (we filled with the mean of the observed values), so “unchanged” proves nothing. But the observed values over-represent new devices (74% of the complete rows), so the mean the AI preserved (about 7791) is already biased relative to the truth (about 7419). Check the group means by device: after mean imputation both groups collapse toward the overall mean. (2) The sd falls (about 2193 vs 2564 truth): the column looks tidier than reality, and every later interval will be too narrow. (3) Legacy users have a true mean of about 5676 steps; mean imputation gives all of their missing rows about 7791, so legacy users appear to walk more than they do, which would flow into any model or score. (4) A better prompt: “The steps are missing more often for legacy devices. Use mice with device and age as predictors, 5 imputations, pmm. Then compare the mean and sd of steps, overall and by device, before and after imputation, and report any group whose mean moves by more than 5%.” Restate: the AI “completed” the column and certified itself. The claim sounds like a check and is not one.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
What was wrong

“Unchanged mean” is guaranteed by the method, so it proves nothing
That mean is already biased: legacy devices are under-represented
The spread shrinks: intervals will be too narrow
Legacy users are filled with the new-device average


A complete column is not a correct column. Compare distributions and groups.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Four things to remember

Parse with a list of orders, count the failures, and never let code guess an ambiguous date.
Impossible first, unusual second. Sentinels and bounds, then z or IQR. Flag, do not delete.
Rules are code. A table of failing counts is a report you can rerun.
Missingness has a pattern. Check who is missing before you drop or fill, and judge imputation by the distribution.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
Unit tests with testthat

library(testthat)

test_that("heart rate is in range after cleaning", {
  expect_true(all(between(clean$hr, 30, 220), na.rm = TRUE))
  expect_equal(sum(clean$hr == -999, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
})

A failing test stops the script. Run it after every cleaning step.

title: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
The slides move fast. This handout is the slow, complete version: read it before class, and return to it when you clean a column.
Session 6 is the second of two sessions on data cleaning. Session 5 covered text. Today covers dates, numbers, and holes: timestamps in many formats, numbers that secretly mean “nothing”, values that are impossible or merely unusual, rules a table must obey, and missing values.
The pattern from Session 5 continues: an AI assistant can make a column look complete or tidy in one line, and quietly damage it. Audit it boxes show these mistakes. The habit to keep is: flag first, fix second, and compare before and after.






The Audit Loop, for numbers and holes




Read the code. What happens to the NA values? To the extremes?
Run it, and compare the summary before and after (counts, mean, spread, group means).
Restate what changed and who it changed for.
Refine it or Reject it. Log the decision.



Setup. The examples use three small files, all on the course site in the data/ folder: s6_vitals.csv (heart rate and steps with sentinels), s6_users.csv (ten records that break known rules), and s6_steps_sim.csv (a simulation, where the true steps are known). You need tidyverse and lubridate (both come with, or alongside, the tidyverse install), and mice for the imputation section.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
vitals    <- read_csv("data/s6_vitals.csv")
users     <- read_csv("data/s6_users.csv")
steps_sim <- read_csv("data/s6_steps_sim.csv")

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
2.1 One column, many formats

ts_raw <- c("2026-01-05 07:30", "01/05/2026 7:30 AM", "5 Jan 2026 07:30",
            "2026-01-05T07:30:00Z", "Jan 5, 2026", "yesterday")
ts_raw

#> [1] "2026-01-05 07:30"     "01/05/2026 7:30 AM"   "5 Jan 2026 07:30"    
#> [4] "2026-01-05T07:30:00Z" "Jan 5, 2026"          "yesterday"


These might come from different devices, from different export tools, or from people typing. A single parsing function only understands the formats it was written for.

ymd_hms(ts_raw, quiet = TRUE)

#> [1] NA                        NA                        NA                       
#> [4] "2026-01-05 07:30:00 UTC" NA                        NA

sum(is.na(ymd_hms(ts_raw, quiet = TRUE)))

#> [1] 5


Five of six values became NA. There was no error. quiet = TRUE hides the warning, but even with the warning, a script that keeps going has silently discarded most of the column.






Audit it: a parser that loses most of the column



An AI may write mutate(ts = ymd_hms(ts_raw)), run it, and move on. After any parse, count the failures: sum(is.na(parsed)) - sum(is.na(original)) is the number of values the parser could not read. If it is more than a handful, the format list is incomplete.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: 2.2 Give it a list of orders
text:
2.2 Give it a list of orders
parse_date_time() takes several orders, each a pattern of date and time pieces: Y year, m month number, b month abbreviation, d day, H hour (24-hour), I hour (12-hour), M minute, p AM/PM, z time zone offset.

parsed <- parse_date_time(ts_raw, tz = "UTC", quiet = TRUE,
  orders = c("Ymd HM", "mdY IMp", "dbY HM", "YmdHMSz", "bdY"))
tibble(ts_raw, parsed, ok = !is.na(parsed))

#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   ts_raw               parsed              ok   
#>   <chr>                <dttm>              <lgl>
#> 1 2026-01-05 07:30     2026-01-05 07:30:00 TRUE 
#> 2 01/05/2026 7:30 AM   2026-01-05 07:30:00 TRUE 
#> 3 5 Jan 2026 07:30     2026-01-05 07:30:00 TRUE 
#> 4 2026-01-05T07:30:00Z 2026-01-05 07:30:00 TRUE 
#> 5 Jan 5, 2026          2026-01-05 00:00:00 TRUE 
#> 6 yesterday            NA                  FALSE


Now inspect what did not parse:

tibble(ts_raw, parsed) |> filter(is.na(parsed))

#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   ts_raw    parsed
#>   <chr>     <dttm>
#> 1 yesterday NA


"yesterday" is not a date, and no list of orders should make it one. It stays NA and gets flagged. Never fill it in with a guess.
Notice also "Jan 5, 2026": it parsed, but with no time, so it became midnight (00:00:00). A missing time of day was turned into a specific time. Whether that matters depends on the analysis, so say it in your log.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
2.3 The day-month trap

d <- c("01/05/2026", "13/05/2026", "05/05/2026", "02/11/2026")
a <- as.numeric(str_extract(d, "^\\d+"))
b <- as.numeric(str_extract(d, "(?<=/)\\d+"))
tibble(d, ambiguous = a <= 12 & b <= 12 & a != b)

#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   d          ambiguous
#>   <chr>      <lgl>    
#> 1 01/05/2026 TRUE     
#> 2 13/05/2026 FALSE    
#> 3 05/05/2026 FALSE    
#> 4 02/11/2026 TRUE


01/05/2026 is January 5 in the US and May 1 in most other places. When both numbers are 12 or less, no code can tell. 13/05/2026 can only be day first, which is a clue that the source uses day first, but a single clue is not proof for the others.

mdy("01/05/2026")

#> [1] "2026-01-05"

dmy("01/05/2026")

#> [1] "2026-05-01"


The honest procedure:

Count how many values are ambiguous.
Look for a clue in the data (a value with a first number above 12, which proves the format).
Ask the source which convention each device or system used, then set the order per source.
If you cannot find out, leave the ambiguous rows NA and flagged.







Audit it: parse_date_time() picks one format for the whole column



If you list both "mdY" and "dmY", lubridate chooses the order that parses the most values in the vector, then applies it to all of them. One unambiguous day-first value such as 13/05/2026 is enough to make the whole column day first, and 01/05/2026 silently becomes May 1, even if it came from a device that writes month first.

x <- c("01/05/2026", "13/05/2026")
parse_date_time(x, orders = c("mdY", "dmY"), quiet = TRUE)

#> [1] "2026-05-01 UTC" "2026-05-13 UTC"


Every value parses and nothing warns you. Parse one source at a time, list only the orders you have evidence for, and keep the ambiguous rows flagged.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
2.4 Time zones

t <- ymd_hms("2026-01-05 07:30:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
t

#> [1] "2026-01-05 07:30:00 PST"

with_tz(t, "UTC")

#> [1] "2026-01-05 15:30:00 UTC"

force_tz(t, "UTC")

#> [1] "2026-01-05 07:30:00 UTC"



with_tz() keeps the instant and changes how it is displayed.
force_tz() keeps the clock reading and changes the zone, which moves the instant. It is for repairing a timestamp that was labeled with the wrong zone.

Mixing them up shifts data by hours. A good default is to store UTC, and convert only for display.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
3.1 Four kinds of “nothing”



Looks like
What it is




NA
R’s missing value


NaN
“not a number”, the result of 0/0


"", "n/a", "NULL"
text pretending to be a value


-999, -1, 9999
a sentinel: a number that means “no data”



NULL is a different thing: it means “no object at all”, and it cannot be an element of a data frame column.

x <- c(1, NA, 0 / 0)
is.na(x)

#> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE

is.nan(x)

#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE


is.na() is TRUE for both NA and NaN. is.nan() is TRUE only for NaN.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
3.2 A sentinel ruins a summary

summary(vitals$hr)

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  -999.0    64.0    72.0    41.2    79.0   300.0


The mean heart rate is about 41. A heart that slow does not exist. The -999 values pulled the mean down, and nothing errored.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: 3.3 Find them: look at the extremes
text:
3.3 Find them: look at the extremes

vitals |>
  filter(hr < 30 | hr > 220) |>
  count(hr, sort = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>      hr     n
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1  -999    29
#> 2     0     8
#> 3   300     4


Three different things share this table: -999 (a sentinel, repeated many times), 0 (impossible, and possibly a failed reading), and 300 (impossible, and possibly a typo). Repetition of one odd value is the signature of a code. A sentinel is a decision someone made when the data was recorded.
A histogram helps too, because a sentinel shows up as an isolated spike far from everything else.

ggplot(vitals, aes(x = hr)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "#6d8d24", color = "white")

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
3.4 Turn sentinels into NA

vit_na <- vitals |> mutate(hr = na_if(hr, -999), steps = na_if(steps, -1))
colSums(is.na(vit_na))

#>    hr steps 
#>    29    25


When you read a file, you can name the sentinels up front:

read_csv("vitals.csv", na = c("", "NA", "n/a", "-999"))







The data dictionary decides



Is -1 a sentinel? In a steps column, yes: nobody walks negative steps. In a temperature column, -1 is a real reading. A pattern cannot tell the difference, and neither can an AI. Check the data dictionary (or ask the source), and write the sentinel list into your code as a decision.








Audit it: filter() deletes the rows, na_if() keeps them



An AI may “remove the bad values” with filter(hr != -999). That deletes entire rows, including their steps, their user, and their timestamp. It also loses the record that the value was missing. Use na_if() (or mutate()) to blank only the bad cell, and keep the row.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: 4.1 Domain bounds: flag, do not delete
text:
4.1 Domain bounds: flag, do not delete

vit <- vit_na |>
  mutate(hr_flag = case_when(is.na(hr) ~ "missing",
                             between(hr, 30, 220) ~ "ok",
                             .default = "impossible"))
count(vit, hr_flag)

#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   hr_flag        n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 impossible    12
#> 2 missing       29
#> 3 ok           959


Two details matter here. The order of case_when() conditions matters: the is.na() test must come first, because between(NA, 30, 220) is NA, not FALSE, and a row with an NA condition falls through to .default. And the row is kept with a flag: a later step decides what to do with "impossible" rows.

c(raw_mean = mean(vitals$hr),
  clean_mean = mean(vit$hr[vit$hr_flag == "ok"]))

#>   raw_mean clean_mean 
#>   41.20000   71.91971


The raw mean was off by about 30 beats per minute, from sentinels alone.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
4.2 z-scores
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\]
A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. For roughly bell-shaped data, about 95% of values fall within 2 and about 99.7% within 3 (the 68-95-99.7 rule), so only about 0.3% are beyond \(|z| > 3\).

hr_ok <- vit |> filter(hr_flag == "ok")
c(n = nrow(hr_ok),
  expected_beyond_3 = round(0.0027 * nrow(hr_ok), 1),
  found = sum(abs(zs(hr_ok$hr)) > 3))

#>                 n expected_beyond_3             found 
#>             959.0               2.6               5.0


The count is close to what a bell curve gives, so nothing here is alarming. A z-score cutoff has to be read against the amount of data: with a million rows you expect about 2,700 values beyond 3.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
4.3 The IQR rule
The interquartile range (IQR) is the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles. A value is flagged if it is more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) below the first quartile or above the third. This is the rule boxplots use for their individual points.

steps_ok <- vit |> filter(!is.na(steps))
ggplot(steps_ok, aes(x = steps)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#cfd82d", outlier.color = "#f68b1f")

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: 4.4 z or IQR? It depends on the shape
text:
4.4 z or IQR? It depends on the shape

tibble(variable   = c("hr (bell-shaped)", "steps (skewed)"),
       z_beyond_3 = c(sum(abs(zs(hr_ok$hr)) > 3), sum(abs(zs(steps_ok$steps)) > 3)),
       iqr_rule   = c(sum(iqr_flag(hr_ok$hr)), sum(iqr_flag(steps_ok$steps))),
       n          = c(nrow(hr_ok), nrow(steps_ok)))

#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>   variable         z_beyond_3 iqr_rule     n
#>   <chr>                 <int>    <int> <int>
#> 1 hr (bell-shaped)          5        8   959
#> 2 steps (skewed)           14       32   975


Steps are skewed: a few very active days stretch a long tail on the right. Both rules flag many of those days, and the IQR rule flags more, but these days are not errors. A z-score assumes a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped variable. For skewed data, look at the plot, and consider transforming (for example, with log()) before applying a rule.






Audit it: “remove outliers” deletes the interesting data



An AI asked to “remove outliers” will often write filter(abs(zs(x)) < 3). On a skewed variable like steps, that removes the long tail of legitimately active users. On a bell-shaped variable, it removes about 0.3% at random. Either way, it makes the column look tidier than reality, and it changes every later summary. Flag instead, then decide for each flagged value: impossible, or merely extreme?

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
4.5 Look in context
For each flagged value, ask three questions.

Impossible? A domain bound says so, and the value is an error: flag it, and decide whether to blank it.
Plausible but extreme? Keep it. It may be your most informative data.
Repeated? The same odd value many times points to a code or a default, not to a person.

Outliers are questions, not verdicts.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
4.6 Odd only in combination
Some values look normal in every column and are impossible together. We simulate height and weight, which move together, and add one record.

set.seed(7)
hw <- tibble(h = round(rnorm(500, 170, 9))) |>
  mutate(w = round(70 + 0.9 * (h - 170) + rnorm(500, 0, 9)))
hw <- bind_rows(hw, tibble(h = 190, w = 45)) |>
  mutate(id = row_number(), zh = zs(h), zw = zs(w),
         bmi = w / (h / 100)^2, zb = zs(bmi),
         md = mahalanobis(cbind(h, w), colMeans(cbind(h, w)), cov(cbind(h, w))))

hw |> filter(id == 501) |> select(h, w, zh, zw, bmi, zb)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>       h     w    zh    zw   bmi    zb
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   190    45  2.17 -2.07  12.5 -3.73


A height of 190 cm and a weight of 45 kg each have \(|z| < 3\). Together they give a BMI of about 12.5, far below the normal range. A derived feature (here, BMI) catches what each column alone cannot.

hw |> filter(abs(zb) > 3) |> select(id, h, w, bmi, zb)

#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>      id     h     w   bmi    zb
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   252   143    30  14.7 -3.02
#> 2   353   158    36  14.4 -3.10
#> 3   449   168    95  33.7  3.14
#> 4   501   190    45  12.5 -3.73


Row 501 is the most extreme, and other rows appear too: with 501 records, a few are expected beyond \(|z| > 3\). Flagged rows are candidates for a look, not automatic errors.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
4.7 Mahalanobis distance (optional)
One distance can summarize several variables at once, accounting for how they move together:
\[D^2 = (x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)\]
For roughly multivariate normal data, \(D^2\) follows a \(\chi^2\) distribution with as many degrees of freedom as variables, which gives a cutoff.

cutoff <- qchisq(.999, df = 2)
round(cutoff, 1)

#> [1] 13.8

hw |> filter(md > cutoff) |> select(id, h, w, md)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>      id     h     w    md
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   501   190    45  27.7


Only the planted record is flagged. This distance assumes roughly normal data, so use it as a screen rather than a test.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
5.1 Dimensions of data quality



Dimension
The question




Validity
Does the data follow its defined rules?


Accuracy
Is it close to the true value?


Consistency
Does it agree with itself and with other tables?


Uniformity
Same units and same format throughout?


Completeness
Is everything we need present?



A value can be valid and still wrong: 120 is a valid heart rate, and it may still be false for that person. Validity is checkable by code. Accuracy usually is not.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: 5.2 Validity rules you can write as code
text:
5.2 Validity rules you can write as code







Rule type
Example




Data type
age is numeric


Range
age between 0 and 120


Mandatory
id is never NA


Unique
id appears once


Set membership
device is watch, band, or ring


Foreign key
every device_id exists in the device table (anti_join())


Pattern
zip is exactly five digits


Cross-field
end is not before start

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
5.3 Rules become counts
Here are the ten users records. Each of the checks below should find something.

users

#> # A tibble: 10 x 6
#>      id   age device zip        start      end       
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <chr>  <chr>      <date>     <date>    
#> 1     1    34 watch  97201      2026-01-01 2026-01-06
#> 2     2    29 band   9720       2026-01-02 2026-01-01
#> 3     3   151 ring   97214      2026-01-03 2026-01-05
#> 4     3    45 watch  97201      2026-01-04 2026-01-03
#> 5     5    -2 Watch  97201-1234 2026-01-05 2026-01-10
#> 6     6    38 band   97005      2026-01-06 2026-01-10
#> 7     7    52 ring   97006      2026-01-07 2026-01-06
#> 8     8    NA watch  97201      2026-01-08 2026-01-11
#> 9    NA    41 band   <NA>       2026-01-09 2026-01-13
#> # i 1 more row



users |>
  summarize(
    id_missing       = sum(is.na(id)),
    id_duplicated    = sum(duplicated(id[!is.na(id)])),
    age_range        = sum(!between(age, 0, 120), na.rm = TRUE),
    device_set       = sum(!device %in% c("watch", "band", "ring")),
    zip_pattern      = sum(!str_detect(zip, "^\\d{5}$"), na.rm = TRUE),
    end_before_start = sum(end < start)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "rule", values_to = "failing")

#> # A tibble: 6 x 2
#>   rule             failing
#>   <chr>              <int>
#> 1 id_missing             1
#> 2 id_duplicated          1
#> 3 age_range              2
#> 4 device_set             2
#> 5 zip_pattern            2
#> 6 end_before_start       4


A table of failing counts is a report you can rerun on every new file. Notice the decisions inside it:

NA age: not out of range. It is missing, which is a different problem. That is why na.rm = TRUE, and why completeness is its own rule.
Duplicated id: the count above is the number of extra copies (1). Counting both copies would give 2. Pick one, and say which.
"Watch": invalid by the rule. You could case-fold first (Session 5) and flag the repair, or flag it as is.
97201-1234: malformed under a five-digit rule, but a valid ZIP+4. Either the rule or the value is wrong, and the data owner decides.







Audit it: a validation function that changes the data



A rule checker should only report. An AI may return a function that also drops the failing rows, fixes the value, or fills it in “to be helpful”. Then the check and the cleaning are fused, and you cannot tell what was changed. Ask for a function that returns a table of rules and counts, and verify that nrow() and the values of the input are unchanged afterwards.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
5.4 Unit tests for cleaning code
testthat turns a rule into a test that stops the script when the data breaks it.

library(testthat)

test_that("heart rate is in range after cleaning", {
  expect_true(all(between(clean$hr, 30, 220), na.rm = TRUE))
  expect_equal(sum(clean$hr == -999, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
})

Run the tests after every cleaning step, and again on every new file. A failing test is cheaper than a wrong model.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
6.1 Why is it missing?








Type
Meaning
Example




Structural
The value cannot exist
“Last pregnancy date” for a man


MCAR (missing completely at random)
Unrelated to anything
A random sync failure


MAR (missing at random)
Related to other columns
Old devices drop steps more often


MNAR (missing not at random)
Related to the missing value itself
Heart rate drops out when it is high



MCAR is rare in real data. MAR and MNAR are the usual cases, and what is safe to do depends on which one you have. (A better name for MAR would be “conditionally at random”: the missingness is random given the other columns.)

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: 6.2 Diagnose: is missingness the same everywhere?
text:
6.2 Diagnose: is missingness the same everywhere?
The method is to make a missingness indicator (TRUE when the value is missing) and compare it across groups.

steps_sim |>
  summarize(missing = mean(is.na(steps)), n = n(), .by = device)

#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   device missing     n
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1 new     0.0798  1203
#> 2 legacy  0.512    797


Legacy devices lose about half of their steps, new devices about 8%. That is not random.

steps_sim |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(age, c(0, 30, 40, 50, Inf))) |>
  summarize(missing = mean(is.na(steps)), n = n(), .by = age_group) |>
  arrange(age_group)

#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>   age_group missing     n
#>   <fct>       <dbl> <int>
#> 1 (0,30]      0.238   407
#> 2 (30,40]     0.295   631
#> 3 (40,50]     0.253   593
#> 4 (50,Inf]    0.193   368
#> 5 <NA>        0         1


By age, the rate is about the same in every group: age is not what drives it here. Comparing groups tells you where to look, and where not to.






Describe, do not prove



A pattern across observed columns can support MAR (missing depends on device). It can never prove MCAR, because you cannot see whether the missing values themselves are different. And it cannot reveal MNAR at all.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
6.3 What dropping the rows does

steps_sim |>
  summarize(all_rows = mean(device == "legacy"),
            complete_rows = mean(device[!is.na(steps)] == "legacy"))

#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   all_rows complete_rows
#>      <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1    0.398         0.260


Legacy devices are about 40% of the users but only about 26% of the complete rows. Dropping rows with NA removes legacy users first, so any model then learns mostly from new-device users. This is a fairness-relevant effect: the people with older devices (often older, or lower income) are quietly underrepresented.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
6.4 MNAR leaves no trace
If heart rate goes missing because it was high (the sensor fails during intense exercise, say), no other column shows it. The data that would reveal it is exactly the data that is missing. Only context can raise the suspicion. What you can do:

ask the source how the sensor behaves,
compare with another source of the same quantity,
run a sensitivity analysis: re-do the analysis under several assumptions about the missing values and see how much the answer changes.


# naniar (optional) gives ready-made missingness plots
library(naniar)
gg_miss_var(steps_sim)       # missing values per column
vis_miss(steps_sim)          # every cell: present or missing

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
section: 7.1 Options, and the rule of thumb
text:
7.1 Options, and the rule of thumb







Option
When it is reasonable




Drop rows
Few are missing (under about 5 to 10%) and the cause looks random


Drop the variable
Mostly missing, and little value


Impute
MAR, and the variable matters


Declare unusable
Too much is missing, or MNAR with no way to check



Percentages like 5 to 10% are rules of thumb, not laws: what matters is who is missing, not only how many. And never impute the label or the outcome you want to predict: that feeds your own guess back in as if it were data.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
7.2 Mean imputation: the tempting one

mean_imp <- steps_sim |>
  mutate(steps = if_else(is.na(steps), mean(steps, na.rm = TRUE), steps))

c(true_sd = sd(steps_sim$steps_true), after_mean_imp = sd(mean_imp$steps))

#>        true_sd after_mean_imp 
#>       2564.128       2193.206


The mean of the column stays where it was, which looks reassuring and proves nothing, because filling with the mean keeps the mean by construction. The spread shrinks: a quarter of the column now holds one repeated value.

bind_rows(truth = steps_sim |> transmute(steps = steps_true),
          `mean imputed` = mean_imp |> select(steps), .id = "version") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = steps, fill = version)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#6d8d24", "#f68b1f"), name = NULL)








The mean-imputed version has a spike at the center and thin tails. Intervals computed from it will be too narrow, and correlations too weak.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
7.3 Multiple imputation with mice
mice (multivariate imputation by chained equations) creates several completed datasets, to carry the uncertainty of not knowing the missing values.

library(mice)
dat <- steps_sim |> select(steps, device, age) |> mutate(device = factor(device))
imp <- mice(dat, m = 5, method = "pmm", donors = 20, printFlag = FALSE, seed = 531)


m = 5: five completed datasets.
method = "pmm" (predictive mean matching): each hole is filled with an observed value taken from a row with a similar prediction, so imputed values are always realistic values.
donors = 20: how many similar rows to draw from. A small donor pool can reuse a few rows over and over.
seed: so you get the same answer when you rerun.

Then analyze each dataset and pool the results. For a simple summary, average across the datasets. For a model, mice pools for you:

fit <- with(imp, lm(steps ~ device + age))
summary(pool(fit))

#>          term  estimate  std.error statistic       df      p.value
#> 1 (Intercept) 8094.8690 200.819735  40.30913 38.48911 4.307036e-33
#> 2   devicenew 3015.5652 115.636787  26.07791 30.31960 2.517706e-22
#> 3         age  -62.4752   4.225107 -14.78665 91.19317 5.954934e-26


pool() combines the five fits using Rubin’s rules, so the standard errors reflect both the usual sampling error and the extra uncertainty from imputation.

title: Session 6 Handout: Types, Anomalies, and Missingness
text:
7.4 Judge it by the distribution
In this simulation we know the true steps, so we can score each method.

stats <- \(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))
pooled <- sapply(1:5, \(i) stats(complete(imp, i)$steps))

rbind(truth           = stats(steps_sim$steps_true),
      `drop rows`     = stats(na.omit(steps_sim$steps)),
      `mean imputed`  = stats(mean_imp$steps),
      `mice (pooled)` = rowMeans(pooled)) |> round()

#>               mean   sd
#> truth         7419 2564
#> drop rows     7791 2536
#> mean imputed  7791 2193
#> mice (pooled) 7404 2604


Dropping rows overstates the mean (the legacy users, who walk less, are missing most). Mean imputation keeps that biased mean and shrinks the spread. mice recovers both.
By group:

by_device <- function(d, nm) d |> summarize(mean = mean(steps), .by = device) |> mutate(version = nm)
bind_rows(
  by_device(steps_sim |> mutate(steps = steps_true), "truth"),
  by_device(steps_sim |> filter(!is.na(steps)), "drop rows"),
  by_device(mean_imp, "mean imputed"),
  by_device(complete(imp, 1) |> as_tibble() |> mutate(device = as.character(device)), "mice (1 of 5)")
) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = device, values_from = mean) |>
  mutate(across(c(legacy, new), round))

#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   version         new legacy
#>   <chr>         <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 truth          8573   5676
#> 2 drop rows      8587   5527
#> 3 mean imputed   8523   6686
#> 4 mice (1 of 5)  8594   5575


Mean imputation gives legacy users the overall average, which is far above what they actually walk, and pulls the two groups toward each other.






With real data there is no truth column



Here we scored against steps_true. Real data never has it. What you can do instead:

Compare the distribution before and after imputation (same shape, same spread?).
Compare group means before and after: does any group move a lot?
Compare imputed values with observed ones: are they plausible for that group?
Run the analysis on several imputed datasets: does the answer change a lot between them?

You can never check a single imputed value against the truth. You can check whether the distribution recovered.








Audit it: a complete column is not a correct column



An AI asked to “fill in the missing steps so the column is complete” returned this:

steps_sim |>
  mutate(steps = if_else(is.na(steps), mean(steps, na.rm = TRUE), steps)) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(steps), sd = sd(steps), missing = sum(is.na(steps)))

#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>    mean    sd missing
#>   <dbl> <dbl>   <int>
#> 1 7791. 2193.       0


and then wrote: “No missing values remain, and the mean is unchanged, so no bias was introduced.” Apply the Audit Loop:

“The mean is unchanged” is guaranteed by the method, so it proves nothing. And that mean is already biased: legacy users, who walk less, are under-represented among the observed values.
The spread shrinks (the standard deviation falls well below the true one), so later intervals will be too narrow.
Legacy users are filled with the average of mostly new-device users.
The claim sounds like a check, but it is not one.

A better prompt: “Steps are missing more often for legacy devices. Use mice with device and age as predictors, five imputations, pmm. Then compare the mean and standard deviation of steps, overall and by device, before and after, and report any group whose mean moves by more than 5%.”

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
The slides move fast. This handout is the slow, complete version: read it before class, and return to it when you clean a column.
Coding session 5 is the first of two sessions on data cleaning. Today covers text: files whose shape is wrong, strings whose content is wrong, and categories that should be one thing and are several. Session 6 covers dates, sentinels, outliers, and missing values.
Cleaning has a hazard that earlier sessions did not: an AI assistant can make a column look clean in one line while it quietly throws information away. Audit it boxes show these mistakes. The habit to build is: count before, count after.






The Audit Loop, for cleaning




Read the code. What does each pattern match, and what could it also match?
Run it on the hard rows (empty, odd, unexpected), not only the easy ones.
Restate what changed: how many rows, which values, and what was lost.
Refine it or Reject it. Log the decision.



Setup. Examples use small inline data, so you can run everything without a download. You need tidyverse (which includes stringr, forcats, and dplyr) and stringi, which stringr installs for you. separate_wider_regex() needs tidyr 1.3.0 or newer, and case_match() needs dplyr 1.1.0 or newer.

library(tidyverse)

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
2.1 Three rules for cleaning code

Code, not clicks. A hand edit in a spreadsheet cannot be repeated or checked.
Re-runnable. Running the whole script twice from raw data gives the same result (this is called an idempotent pipeline).
Every fix is logged. What changed, how many rows, and why.







Key idea



Every cleaning step is a decision that changes what a model will learn. If you cannot say what a step removed or changed, you have not finished the step.

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
2.2 Structural and content grime







Structural
Content




The shape of the file is wrong
The values in cells are wrong


Shows up at import
Shows up at inspection


Extra or missing fields, bad delimiters, encoding
Typos, mixed units, sentinels, lookalikes


Often needs a manual rule
Often needs a lookup table



Handle structural problems first: content checks assume a clean grid.

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
2.3 Versioning data as you work
How you keep track of changes depends on size.







Size of data
Approach




Fits easily in memory
Create a new object at each step; the script is the history


Large
Edit in place and log each change in a text column or file


Massive
Do not load it all; sample, process in chunks, or push computation to the database (see arrow in Session 2)

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
4.1 The building blocks








Piece
Meaning
Example




\\d \\w \\s
a digit, a word character, a whitespace
\\d{5} is five digits


.
any one character
a.c matches abc, a-c


+ * ?
one or more, zero or more, optional
\\d+ is a run of digits


{3} {2,4}
exactly 3, between 2 and 4
\\d{3}-\\d{4}


^ $
start, end of the string
^\\d+$ is only digits


( ) \|
group, alternatives
kg\|lbs?


[abc] [^abc]
one of these, none of these
[^0-9] is a non-digit



In an R string the backslash must be doubled: "\\d+". A raw string avoids the doubling: r"(\d+)".

# These two patterns are the same
str_extract("room 204", "\\d+")

#> [1] "204"

str_extract("room 204", r"(\d+)")

#> [1] "204"

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
4.2 See what a pattern matches
str_view() highlights the match, which makes patterns much easier to debug.

str_view(body$weight_raw, "\\d+\\.?\\d*")

#> [1] | <165> lb
#> [2] | <72>kg
#> [3] | <80> KG
#> [4] | <170>
#> [6] | <154.5> lbs
#> [7] | <68> kg

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
4.3 Our messy column

body

#> # A tibble: 7 x 2
#>      id weight_raw
#>   <int> <chr>     
#> 1     1 165 lb    
#> 2     2 72kg      
#> 3     3 80 KG     
#> 4     4 170       
#> 5     5 n/a       
#> 6     6 154.5 lbs 
#> 7     7 68 kg


These weights were typed by humans: different units (lb, lbs, kg, KG), different spacing, one row with a number and no unit, and one with no number at all.

4.3.1 Which rows: str_detect()

body |>
  mutate(has_lb = str_detect(weight_raw, regex("lbs?", ignore_case = TRUE)))

#> # A tibble: 7 x 3
#>      id weight_raw has_lb
#>   <int> <chr>      <lgl> 
#> 1     1 165 lb     TRUE  
#> 2     2 72kg       FALSE 
#> 3     3 80 KG      FALSE 
#> 4     4 170        FALSE 
#> 5     5 n/a        FALSE 
#> 6     6 154.5 lbs  TRUE  
#> 7     7 68 kg      FALSE


str_detect() returns TRUE or FALSE. Use it inside filter() to keep rows, or in mutate() to flag them. regex(..., ignore_case = TRUE) makes the match case-insensitive.


4.3.2 What is in them: str_extract()

body |>
  mutate(
    num = as.numeric(str_extract(weight_raw, "\\d+\\.?\\d*")),
    unit = str_extract(str_to_lower(weight_raw), "kg|lbs?")
  )

#> # A tibble: 7 x 4
#>      id weight_raw   num unit 
#>   <int> <chr>      <dbl> <chr>
#> 1     1 165 lb      165  lb   
#> 2     2 72kg         72  kg   
#> 3     3 80 KG        80  kg   
#> 4     4 170         170  <NA> 
#> 5     5 n/a          NA  <NA> 
#> 6     6 154.5 lbs   154. lbs  
#> 7     7 68 kg        68  kg


Read the number pattern aloud: “one or more digits, then an optional dot, then zero or more digits”. When nothing matches, you get NA, not an error. Row 4 has a number (170) and no unit, and row 5 has neither.


4.3.3 Convert, and leave the unknown unknown

body |>
  mutate(
    num = as.numeric(str_extract(weight_raw, "\\d+\\.?\\d*")),
    unit = str_extract(str_to_lower(weight_raw), "kg|lbs?"),
    kg = case_when(unit == "kg" ~ num, str_detect(unit, "lb") ~ num * 0.453592)
  )

#> # A tibble: 7 x 5
#>      id weight_raw   num unit     kg
#>   <int> <chr>      <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1     1 165 lb      165  lb     74.8
#> 2     2 72kg         72  kg     72  
#> 3     3 80 KG        80  kg     80  
#> 4     4 170         170  <NA>   NA  
#> 5     5 n/a          NA  <NA>   NA  
#> 6     6 154.5 lbs   154. lbs    70.1
#> 7     7 68 kg        68  kg     68


case_when() with no default returns NA for rows that match no condition. Here that is the right behavior: 170 could be pounds or kilograms, and a regex cannot know which. Staying NA (and flagged) is better than a guess that is hidden inside a pattern.






Audit it: parse_number() ignores units



parse_number() is tempting because it is one line.

body |> mutate(shortcut = c(parse_number(weight_raw)))

#> # A tibble: 7 x 3
#>      id weight_raw shortcut
#>   <int> <chr>         <dbl>
#> 1     1 165 lb         165 
#> 2     2 72kg            72 
#> 3     3 80 KG           80 
#> 4     4 170            170 
#> 5     5 n/a             NA 
#> 6     6 154.5 lbs      154.
#> 7     7 68 kg           68


It returns 165, 72, 80 and 170 as if they shared a unit. Pounds and kilograms are now mixed in one numeric column, and nothing warns you (the one warning is for n/a). Extract the unit as well as the number, and decide about the rows without a unit.




4.3.4 Replace and tidy: str_replace() and friends

c("  Portland ", "Portland,  OR", "portland") |>
  str_squish() |>
  str_remove(",\\s*OR$") |>
  str_to_title()

#> [1] "Portland" "Portland" "Portland"



str_squish() trims both ends and collapses runs of spaces inside.
str_remove(x, pattern) is str_replace(x, pattern, "").
str_replace() changes the first match, str_replace_all() changes every match.
str_to_lower(), str_to_upper(), str_to_title() change case.







Audit it: the dot matches anything



An AI asked to “remove the dots from a phone number” may write:

str_replace_all("503.555.0142", ".", "")

#> [1] ""


The result is an empty string. In a regex, . means “any character”, so every character was removed. Escape it ("\\."), put it in a class ("[.]"), or match it literally with fixed(".").

str_replace_all("503.555.0142", fixed("."), "")

#> [1] "5035550142"










Audit it: str_extract() returns only the first match



“Pull the numbers out of 5 ft 11 in” with str_extract(x, "\\d+") returns "5" and drops the 11. Use str_extract_all() (which returns a list) or capture each piece on purpose, as below.

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
4.4 Capture groups: separate_wider_regex()
When a string has several parts, name each one. Unnamed pieces are matched and dropped; named pieces become columns.

tibble(height_raw = c("5 ft 11 in", "5ft 7in", "6 ft 0 in")) |>
  separate_wider_regex(
    height_raw,
    c(ft = "\\d", "\\s*ft\\s*", inch = "\\d+", ".*")
  )

#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   ft    inch 
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 5     11   
#> 2 5     7    
#> 3 6     0


If a string does not fit the pattern, the function stops with an error by default. That is a feature: it tells you the pattern is incomplete. Options such as too_few = "align_start" let rows through when you decide that is acceptable.

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
4.5 Lookarounds (optional)
A lookahead checks what comes next without consuming it. The pattern "^1(?=\\d{10}$)" means “a leading 1, but only if exactly ten digits follow”. It is how clean_phone() below strips a US country code without breaking a seven-digit number that happens to start with 1.

str_remove("15035550142", "^1(?=\\d{10}$)")

#> [1] "5035550142"

str_remove("1503555", "^1(?=\\d{10}$)")

#> [1] "1503555"

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
5.1 Detect
Any character outside plain ASCII (code points 0 to 127) matches [^\\x00-\\x7F].

str_detect(c(good, bad), "[^\\x00-\\x7F]")

#> [1] FALSE  TRUE

stringi::stri_escape_unicode(bad)

#> [1] "gr\\u0435\\u0435n"


stri_escape_unicode() shows each non-ASCII character as its \uXXXX code. To find every offending row in a table:

tibble(city = c("Portland", "\u0420ortland", "Beaverton")) |>
  filter(str_detect(city, "[^\\x00-\\x7F]"))

#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   city    
#>   <chr>   
#> 1 Рortland








Audit it: look-alikes break joins without an error




lookup <- tibble(
  color = c("blue", "red", "green"),
  hex = c("#00f", "#f00", "#0a0")
)

tibble(color = c("blue", "green", bad)) |>
  anti_join(lookup, by = "color")

#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   color
#>   <chr>
#> 1 grееn


The join does not fail. The lookalike simply does not match, and it will be missing from every result built on that join. Run anti_join() against your lookup tables as a routine check (Session 2).

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
5.2 Decide whether to normalize
stringi::stri_trans_general() can transliterate text.

stringi::stri_trans_general(c(bad, "caf\u00e9"), "Any-Latin; Latin-ASCII")

#> [1] "green" "cafe"


The Cyrillic е became a Latin e, which is what we wanted. But café also became cafe. Whether that is acceptable depends on the column: for a color, yes; for a person’s name, ask first. Detect first, then decide. Real data also contains legitimate non-ASCII text (José, Zoë), so “non-ASCII” is a flag for review, not proof of an error.

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
5.3 Invisible characters

x <- c("blue", "blue\u00a0", "blue\u200b")
nchar(x)

#> [1] 4 5 5

nchar(str_squish(x))

#> [1] 4 4 5


str_squish() removes the non-breaking space (\u00a0) but not the zero-width space (\u200b), which has length but no width. If two strings look identical and are not equal, compare nchar() and stri_escape_unicode().

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
6.1 Case-fold and trim

humans |>
  mutate(favorite = str_to_lower(str_squish(favorite))) |>
  count(favorite, sort = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 7 x 2
#>   favorite       n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 blue          42
#> 2 red           33
#> 3 green         25
#> 4 gray           4
#> 5 blüe           1
#> 6 chartreuse     1
#> 7 grееn          1


Two problems are gone: Red merged with red, and " blue" merged with blue. What is left: blüe, the Cyrillic green, and chartreuse.






Case folding is not always safe



Case carries no meaning for a color, but it might for an identifier.

ids <- c("ab12", "AB12")
n_distinct(ids)

#> [1] 2

n_distinct(str_to_lower(ids))

#> [1] 1


Fold case only where case carries no meaning, and say so in your log.

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
section: 6.2 Fix known variants with a lookup table
text:
6.2 Fix known variants with a lookup table

fixes <- tribble(
  ~raw              , ~clean  ,
  "bl\u00fce"       , "blue"  ,
  "gr\u0435\u0435n" , "green"
)

humans |>
  mutate(favorite = str_to_lower(str_squish(favorite))) |>
  left_join(fixes, by = c("favorite" = "raw")) |>
  mutate(favorite = coalesce(clean, favorite)) |>
  count(favorite, sort = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   favorite       n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 blue          43
#> 2 red           33
#> 3 green         26
#> 4 gray           4
#> 5 chartreuse     1


Why a table and not a chain of ifelse() calls:

A reviewer can read it in ten seconds.
It is data: you can version it, diff it, and extend it.
anti_join() shows what is still unmapped.
It works on next month’s file.

For a few mappings, case_match() is a compact alternative:

humans |>
  mutate(
    favorite = str_to_lower(str_squish(favorite)),
    favorite = case_match(
      favorite,
      "bl\u00fce" ~ "blue",
      "gr\u0435\u0435n" ~ "green",
      .default = favorite
    )
  ) |>
  count(favorite, sort = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   favorite       n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 blue          43
#> 2 red           33
#> 3 green         26
#> 4 gray           4
#> 5 chartreuse     1


The .default = favorite keeps every value you did not mention. Without it, unmatched values silently become NA.

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
6.4 Grouping valid levels: fct_collapse()

humans |>
  mutate(
    favorite = str_to_lower(str_squish(favorite)),
    group = fct_collapse(
      favorite,
      cool = c("blue", "green"),
      warm = "red",
      other_level = "other"
    )
  ) |>
  count(group)

#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   group     n
#>   <fct> <int>
#> 1 cool     67
#> 2 warm     33
#> 3 other     7


fct_collapse() and fct_lump_*() are for grouping valid levels when you want fewer categories for analysis. They are not repair tools: they hide the very values you needed to look at.






Audit it: fct_lump_min() makes a table shorter, not cleaner



An AI asked to “standardize the favorite color column” returned this:

humans |>
  mutate(favorite = str_to_lower(favorite)) |>
  mutate(favorite = fct_lump_min(favorite, min = 2, other_level = "other")) |>
  count(favorite, sort = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 6 x 2
#>   favorite     n
#>   <fct>    <int>
#> 1 "blue"      40
#> 2 "red"       33
#> 3 "green"     25
#> 4 "gray"       4
#> 5 "other"      3
#> 6 " blue"      2


Compare with the counts at the start of this section:

Lost counts: 43 people said blue (blue, " blue", blüe), but blue shows 40. Green shows 25, not 26.
"other" (3) hides three different things: a typo (blüe), a lookalike (grееn), and a real rare color (chartreuse).
No str_squish(): " blue" is still its own level.
No log: nothing says what moved where.

The AI cleaned the output, not the data. The better prompt asks for trimming, lowercasing, a lookup table of known fixes, and a list of every value still outside the valid set, with the instruction not to lump or delete.

title: Session 5 Handout: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
7.1 Prompting from a spec
A good prompt for code like this:

Pastes the spec table in as text.
Says what the function takes and returns (“a character vector in, a character vector of the same length out”).
Forbids guessing: “return NA when the input does not match, never a default”.
Asks for tidyverse code only, and no extra packages.

Then run the spec. A failing row is a gift: add it to the spec (and fix the function). The spec grows with every surprise in real data.

Code, not clicks. No hand edits in a spreadsheet.
Re-runnable. Run the whole script twice: same result.

Structural

Size

title: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
A pattern, not a literal



Piece
Meaning




\\d \\w \\s
digit, word character, space


+ * ?
one or more, zero or more, optional


{3} {2,4}
exactly 3, between 2 and 4


^ $
start, end of the string


( ) \|
group, or


[^...]
anything except these



In R strings the backslash doubles: "\\d+". Or use a raw string: r"(\d+)".

text:
Task 1: code it
Convert weight_raw to kilograms. Pounds times 0.453592.

Code it (5 min). Add a column kg. Rows with no unit must stay NA, not be guessed. Check all 7 rows.


body |>
  mutate(num = ..., unit = ..., kg = ...)


TASK 1 of 3 (CODE IT). Give 5 minutes; walk the room. Expected: num <- as.numeric(str_extract(weight_raw, “\d+\.?\d”)); unit <- str_extract(str_to_lower(weight_raw), ”kg|lbs?”); kg <- case_when(unit == ”kg” ~ num, str_detect(unit, ”lb”) ~ num  0.453592). Result: 74.8, 72, 80, NA, NA, 70.1, 68. Common stuck points: forgetting str_to_lower so”KG” fails to match, regex written “” with one backslash, case_when with no default (NA is the right default here, say so), str_detect(NA, …) returning NA. Early finishers: add a column flag that says why a row is NA (“no unit”, “no number”). Key point to land: the row “170” is NOT 170 kg and NOT 170 lb. We do not know, so it stays NA and is flagged. A guess would be a decision hidden inside a regex.

Same look, different string

good <- "green"
bad <- "gr\u0435\u0435n" # two Cyrillic letters that look like e

stringi::stri_trans_general(c(bad, "caf\u00e9"), "Any-Latin; Latin-ASCII")

The Cyrillic е became e. But café became cafe too.

title: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
Count first

Task 2: prompt it
Raw city values from a signup form:
"Portland", "portland ", "PORTLAND", "Portland, OR", "Portlnd", "Beaverton", "beaverton", "Port land"

Prompt it (7 min). 1. Write the spec table: what should each become? 2. Prompt your AI for clean_city(). 3. Run your spec against it.

Decide what Portlnd and Port land should become. Then say why in your prompt.

TASK 2 of 3 (PROMPT IT). Give 7 minutes: about 2 for the spec table, 3 for prompting, 2 for running it. Expected from the room: the first four and the Beaverton pair become “Portland” and “Beaverton”. The hard rows are “Portlnd” and “Port land”: they need a LOOKUP of known cities (or fuzzy matching with a threshold) and a flag, not a guess. A good prompt includes the spec table pasted in, says the function takes and returns a character vector, forbids guessing (unmatched becomes NA), and asks for tidyverse code only. What often goes wrong: the AI returns a function that title-cases everything (so “Port land” becomes “Port Land” and nobody notices), or adds a fuzzy-matching package without being asked, or silently maps “Portlnd” with a default. All of these show up as failing spec rows, which is the point. Collect two spec tables that disagree about “Port land” and let the room argue: that disagreement IS the cleaning decision, and it belongs in the spec, written down, before any code.

How many real blues and greens did we lose?

What would you ask for instead?


TASK 3 of 3 (ASSESS IT). Give 4 minutes. Findings: (1) blue shows 40 but there are 43 people who said blue (blüe and ” blue” are not merged); green shows 25 but there are 26. (2) “other” (3) is a mix of a typo (blüe), a lookalike (grееn) and a real rare color (chartreuse): fct_lump_min turned three different problems into one anonymous bucket. (3) ” blue” with a leading space is still its own level because there was no str_squish; the table looks tidy but the grime is still there, just renamed. (4) Better prompt: “Trim, lowercase, then apply this lookup table of known fixes; list every value that is still not in the valid set; do not lump or delete.” Restate: the AI cleaned the OUTPUT, not the DATA: the table is shorter, and information was destroyed.

title: Strings, Unicode, and Categories
text:
Four things to remember

Flag, then fix. Every fix is a decision; log it.
Regex: read it aloud, and test it on the rows that look wrong. NA means “no match”, not “no problem”.
Look-alikes are real. Detect non-ASCII, then decide whether to normalize.
Spec first. Write inputs and expected outputs, then let the table judge the AI.
